arXiv:2407.07459v2 [math.GR] 11 Sep 2024

Retraction to a parabolic subgroup and applications

François Digne, Eddy Godelle and Jean Michel
Abstract.

We continue the study of the retraction from an Artin group to a standard parabolic subgroup introduced by Blufstein, Charney, Paris and the second author. Using right and left retractions we obtain new results on minimal parabolic subgroups, intersection of parabolic subgroups, double cosets with respect to parabolic subgroups and conjugacy classes in Artin groups.

0. Introduction

Given a non-empty set SS, a Coxeter matrix is a symmetric matrix (ms,t)s,t∈S(m_{s,t})_{s,t\in S} such that ms,s=1m_{s,s}=1 and ms,t∈ℕ≥2∪{∞}m_{s,t}\in{\mathbb{N}}_{\geq 2}\cup\{\infty\} for s≠ts\neq t. To such a Coxeter matrix one can associate a group, namely its associated Coxeter group, defined by the following presentation

(∗) W=⟨S|s2=1 for s∈Ssts⋯⏟ms,t​ terms=tst⋯⏟ms,t​ terms for ​s≠t​ and ​ms,t≠∞⟩W=\biggl\langle S\ \biggl|\ \begin{array}[]{cl}s^{2}=1&\textrm{ for }s\in S\\ \underbrace{sts\cdots}_{m_{s,t}\textrm{ terms}}=\underbrace{tst\cdots}_{m_{s,t}\textrm{ terms}}&\textrm{ for }s\neq t\textrm{ and }m_{s,t}\neq\infty\end{array}\biggr\rangle

Given a copy 𝐒{\mathbf{S}} of SS one can also define the associated Artin group

(∗∗) B=⟨𝐒|𝐬𝐭𝐬⋯⏟ms,t​ terms=𝐭𝐬𝐭⋯⏟ms,t​ terms for s≠t and ms,t≠∞⟩B=\biggl\langle{\mathbf{S}}\ \biggl|\ \underbrace{{\mathbf{s}}{\mathbf{t}}{\mathbf{s}}\cdots}_{m_{s,t}\textrm{ terms}}=\underbrace{{\mathbf{t}}{\mathbf{s}}{\mathbf{t}}\cdots}_{m_{s,t}\textrm{ terms}}\textrm{ for }s\neq t\textrm{ and }m_{s,t}\neq\infty\biggr\rangle

We denote by B+B^{+} the submonoid of BB generated by 𝐒{\mathbf{S}}; its elements are called positive braids. We denote the length on WW with respect to SS by ℓS:W→ℕ\ell_{S}:W\to{\mathbb{N}} and we denote by ℓℤ:B→ℤ{\ell_{{\mathbb{Z}}}}:B\to{\mathbb{Z}} the group morphism which sends 𝐒{\mathbf{S}} to 11. It immediately follows from the presentations that the map 𝐬∈𝐒↦s∈S{\mathbf{s}}\in{\mathbf{S}}\mapsto s\in S induces a morphism pr:B→W\pr:B\to W. Its kernel is called the pure Artin group associated to BB (or the coloured Artin group) and will be denoted by PP. Moreover, the inverse bijection s↦𝐬s\mapsto{\mathbf{s}} extends by lifting reduced expressions to a canonical section (of sets) from WW to BB. In the sequel 𝐖{\mathbf{W}} will denote the image of this section. This is a subset of B+B^{+}. The elements of 𝐖{\mathbf{W}} are called simple braids. We will use the following notations: for 𝐰∈𝐖{\mathbf{w}}\in{\mathbf{W}} the notation ww means pr⁡(𝐰)\pr({\mathbf{w}}) and for w∈Ww\in W the notation 𝐰{\mathbf{w}} means the lift of ww to 𝐖{\mathbf{W}}. In other words 𝐰{\mathbf{w}} is the unique element in B+B^{+} such that pr⁡(𝐰)=w\pr({\mathbf{w}})=w and ℓℤ​(𝐰)=ℓS​(w){\ell_{{\mathbb{Z}}}}({\mathbf{w}})=\ell_{S}(w).

Many papers focus on Artin groups, but whereas Coxeter groups are almost well-understood, this is not the case for Artin groups. Even the word problem remains open in general. The strategy used to prove most of the results obtained is to use a particular family of subgroups, namely the family of standard parabolic subgroups. This is why in [5] the authors claim that “any result on these subgroups is likely to be useful”. For I⊆SI\subseteq S, the standard parabolic subgroup BIB_{I} (resp. WIW_{I}) of BB (resp. of WW) is the subgroup generated by 𝐈⊆𝐒{\mathbf{I}}\subseteq{\mathbf{S}} lifting II (resp. generated by II). Such a subgroup is an Artin group (resp. a Coxeter group) for the submatrix (ms,t)s,t∈I(m_{s,t})_{s,t\in I} (cf. [19], see also Proposition 2.5). A parabolic subgroup is any subgroup that is conjugate to a standard parabolic subgroup.

The present article studies the properties of a retraction on standard parabolic subgroups which has been defined in [2]. This is a continuation of a series of articles [15, 5, 2, 14] on this topic. A complex Sal​(B)\textrm{Sal}(B), called the Salvetti complex, can be associated with each Artin group. Furthermore, for every standard parabolic subgroup BIB_{I} there exists a canonical embedding Sal​(BI)→Sal​(B)\textrm{Sal}(B_{I})\to\textrm{Sal}(B). In [15], the authors prove that this embedding admits a retraction. Then in [5, Theorem 1.2], the authors use the above retraction to prove that standard parabolic subgroups of Artin groups are convex (see also Proposition 4.7). Along the way, they use the above retraction to construct a retraction 𝝅I\bpi_{I} from the Artin group BB to its standard parabolic subgroup BIB_{I}. The construction was implicit in the proof of the main result of [5] and is made explicit in [2]. In [14] an alternative construction of this retraction is obtained, which is based only on algebraic and elementary arguments; several algebraic properties of the retraction are also obtained.

The present article will take this approach further. One of the aims is to relate the definition of the retraction to root systems and make it sufficiently explicit that it is easy to calculate. The retraction is not a morphism, and a goal is to better understand the retraction of a product. In particular, we extend results of [2, 14]. We recall that B+B^{+} is a locally Garside monoid; each element 𝐛∈B+{\mathbf{b}}\in B^{+} has a so-called Garside normal form which is the unique sequence (𝐛1,…,𝐛n)({\mathbf{b}}_{1},\ldots,{\mathbf{b}}_{n}) such that 𝐛=𝐛1​…​𝐛n{\mathbf{b}}={\mathbf{b}}_{1}\ldots{\mathbf{b}}_{n} where 𝐛i{\mathbf{b}}_{i} is the greatest left-divisor of 𝐛i​…​𝐛n{\mathbf{b}}_{i}\ldots{\mathbf{b}}_{n} in B+B^{+} which is in 𝐖{\mathbf{W}} and n≥0n\geq 0 is minimal. The following proposition summarises some of our results on the retraction of a product (we postpone the definition of reduced elements and of the morphism φpr⁡(𝐛)\varphi_{\pr({\mathbf{b}})} to the next sections).

Let BB be an Artin group and BIB_{I} be a standard parabolic subgroup for some I⊆SI\subseteq S. Let 𝐛{\mathbf{b}} be in BB.

  1. (1)

    (Proposition 2.6(7)) If pr⁡(𝐛)∈WI\pr({\mathbf{b}})\in W_{I} then for 𝐛′∈B{\mathbf{b}}^{\prime}\in B we have 𝝅I⁡(𝐛𝐛′)=𝝅I⁡(𝐛)​𝝅I⁡(𝐛′)\bpi_{I}({\mathbf{b}}{\mathbf{b}}^{\prime})=\bpi_{I}({\mathbf{b}})\bpi_{I}({\mathbf{b}}^{\prime}).

  2. (2)

    (Proposition 2.6(9)) Assume for J⊆SJ\subseteq S that pr⁡(𝐛)\pr({\mathbf{b}}) is II-reduced-JJ. Then for 𝐣∈BJ{\mathbf{j}}\in B_{J} we have 𝝅I⁡(𝐛𝐣)=𝝅I⁡(𝐛)​φpr⁡(𝐛)​(𝝅J1⁡(𝐣))\bpi_{I}({\mathbf{b}}{\mathbf{j}})=\bpi_{I}({\mathbf{b}})\varphi_{\pr({\mathbf{b}})}(\bpi_{J_{1}}({\mathbf{j}})) where J1=Ipr⁡(𝐛)∩JJ_{1}=I^{\pr({\mathbf{b}})}\cap J.

Then, m≤nm\leq n and for 1≤i≤m1\leq i\leq m, the element 𝝅I(𝐛1⋯𝐛i)\bpi_{I}({\mathbf{b}}_{1}\cdots{\mathbf{b}}_{i}) left divides 𝐢1⋯𝐢i{\mathbf{i}}_{1}\cdots{\mathbf{i}}_{i}.

In the next proposition we consider the case of Artin groups of spherical type, that is when WW is finite. In this case WW has a unique longest element relative to ℓS\ell_{S}. Its lift in 𝐖{\mathbf{W}}, denoted by Δ\Delta, is a Garside element of B+B^{+}. For I⊆SI\subseteq S, the corresponding element of BI+B^{+}_{I} lifting the longest element of WIW_{I} is denoted by ΔI\Delta_{I}.

Proposition 0.2.

(Proposition 2.12) Assume WW is finite. Then for any 𝐛∈B{\mathbf{b}}\in B, I⊆SI\subseteq S and i∈ℤi\in{\mathbb{Z}} we have 𝛑I⁡(𝐛​Δi)=𝛑I⁡(𝐛)​𝛑I⁡(Δi)=𝛑I⁡(𝐛)​ΔIi\bpi_{I}({\mathbf{b}}\Delta^{i})=\bpi_{I}({\mathbf{b}})\bpi_{I}(\Delta^{i})=\bpi_{I}({\mathbf{b}})\Delta_{I}^{i}.

For 𝐛∈B{\mathbf{b}}\in B, define 𝐭I​(𝐛){\mathbf{t}}_{I}({\mathbf{b}}) by 𝐛=𝝅I⁡(𝐛)​𝐭I​(𝐛){\mathbf{b}}=\bpi_{I}({\mathbf{b}}){\mathbf{t}}_{I}({\mathbf{b}}). Then, the map 𝐛↦𝐭I​(𝐛){\mathbf{b}}\mapsto{\mathbf{t}}_{I}({\mathbf{b}}) gives a transversal of the right coset BI​𝐛B_{I}{\mathbf{b}} in BB (see Proposition 2.9). Exchanging left and right, one can define a right retraction 𝝅Ir⁡(𝐛)\bpi^{r}_{I}({\mathbf{b}}) such that 𝐛=tIr​(𝐛)​𝝅Ir⁡(𝐛){\mathbf{b}}=t^{r}_{I}({\mathbf{b}})\bpi^{r}_{I}({\mathbf{b}}) and 𝐛↦tIr​(𝐛){\mathbf{b}}\mapsto t^{r}_{I}({\mathbf{b}}) gives a transversal of the left coset 𝐛​BI{\mathbf{b}}B_{I} in BB. These two retractions are closely related (see Proposition 3.1). We use them to address the question of how to solve the double coset problem in Artin groups. A solution to the double coset problem for Coxeter groups is known since [3]: every double coset has a unique element of minimal length which is easy to compute starting from any (word representing an) element of the double coset. Very few results have been obtained for Artin groups. The only result on the subject known to the authors is in the unpublished article [16]. It gives a partial answer in the case of braid groups, that is when WW is of type AA. Using left and right retractions, we obtain a partial result with the same flavour as in the case of Coxeter groups:

Proposition 0.3.

Let I,J⊆SI,J\subseteq S and 𝐛∈B{\mathbf{b}}\in B be such that WJpr⁡(𝐛)∩WI={1}\kern 0.5pt\vphantom{W}{}^{\pr({\mathbf{b}})}\kern-0.5ptW_{J}\cap W_{I}=\{1\}. Then the element 𝐛0=𝐭Jr​(𝐭I​(𝐛))=𝐭I​(𝐭Jr​(𝐛)){\mathbf{b}}_{0}={\mathbf{t}}_{J}^{r}({\mathbf{t}}_{I}({\mathbf{b}}))={\mathbf{t}}_{I}({\mathbf{t}}_{J}^{r}({\mathbf{b}})) is the unique element of BI​𝐛​BJB_{I}{\mathbf{b}}B_{J} such that 𝛑I⁡(𝐛0)=𝛑Jr⁡(𝐛0)=1\bpi_{I}({\mathbf{b}}_{0})=\bpi_{J}^{r}({\mathbf{b}}_{0})=1.

This is proved after Remark 3.10 as a consequence of that remark and of the more general result Corollary 3.9.

It is a conjecture that the intersection of any two parabolic subgroups is a parabolic subgroup. The validity of the conjecture is proved for several families of Artin groups [1, 6, 7, 8, 17] but remains open in general. Using the retraction we address the conjecture and we show that starting from any element 𝐛{\mathbf{b}} in BB, the study of BI∩𝐛BJB_{I}\cap\kern 0.5pt\vphantom{B}^{{\mathbf{b}}}\kern-0.5ptB_{J} can be reduced to the case where 𝐛=𝐩{\mathbf{b}}={\mathbf{p}} is in PP and J=IJ=I (see Proposition 3.12). In this case we prove

Proposition 0.4.

Let II be a subset of SS and 𝐩{\mathbf{p}} be in PP such that πI​(𝐩)=1\pi_{I}({\mathbf{p}})=1; then

BI∩𝐩BI=CBI(𝐩)B_{I}\cap\kern 0.5pt\vphantom{B}^{{\mathbf{p}}}\kern-0.5ptB_{I}=C_{B_{I}}({\mathbf{p}})

where CBI​(𝐩)={𝐛∈BI∣𝐩𝐛=𝐛𝐩}C_{B_{I}}({\mathbf{p}})=\{{\mathbf{b}}\in B_{I}\mid{\mathbf{p}}{\mathbf{b}}={\mathbf{b}}{\mathbf{p}}\}, the centraliser of 𝐩{\mathbf{p}} in BIB_{I}.

One of the main long-standing open problems for braid groups is the existence of a polynomial-time algorithm for the conjugacy problem. The partial results obtained on the subject are related to the Nielsen-Thurston classification (reducible, periodic or pseudo-Anosov) of braids. The conjugacy problem, and even the word problem remain open in the general case. In the last part of the article, we focus on the study of the conjugacy class of an element. In the spirit of the Nielsen-Thurston classification, we focus on what might be called “reducible” elements.

Denote by ℓ𝐒±1:B→ℕ{\ell_{{\mathbf{S}}^{\pm 1}}}:B\to{\mathbb{N}} the length function on BB with respect to the generating set 𝐒±1{\mathbf{S}}^{\pm 1}. For 𝐛∈B{\mathbf{b}}\in B, it is equal to ℓ⁡(b){\ell}(b), the length of any minimal word b∈(𝐒±1)∗b\in({\mathbf{S}}^{\pm 1})^{*} representing 𝐛{\mathbf{b}}. By convexity any such word bb is written on the same set 𝐈⊆𝐒{\mathbf{I}}\subseteq{\mathbf{S}}, the image I⊆SI\subseteq S of which we call the support of 𝐛{\mathbf{b}}, denoted by supp⁡(𝐛)\supp({\mathbf{b}}). The following result is a part of Propositions 4.8, 4.12 and Corollary 4.11.

Proposition 0.5.

Let 𝐛∈B{\mathbf{b}}\in B and let ConjB⁡(𝐛)\conj_{B}({\mathbf{b}}) denote the conjugacy class of 𝐛{\mathbf{b}}.

  1. (1)

    For I⊆SI\subseteq S, either ConjB⁡(𝐛)∩BI\conj_{B}({\mathbf{b}})\cap B_{I} is empty or it contains an element 𝐡{\mathbf{h}} such that ℓ𝐒±1​(𝐡){\ell_{{\mathbf{S}}^{\pm 1}}}({\mathbf{h}}) is minimal in ConjB⁡(𝐛)\conj_{B}({\mathbf{b}}).

  2. (2)

    If ℓ𝐒±1​(𝐛){\ell_{{\mathbf{S}}^{\pm 1}}}({\mathbf{b}}) is minimal in Conj⁡(𝐛)\conj({\mathbf{b}}) and if 𝐛′∈Conj⁡(𝐛){\mathbf{b}}^{\prime}\in\conj({\mathbf{b}}) satisfies ℓ𝐒±1​(𝐛′)=ℓ𝐒±1​(𝐛){\ell_{{\mathbf{S}}^{\pm 1}}}({\mathbf{b}}^{\prime})={\ell_{{\mathbf{S}}^{\pm 1}}}({\mathbf{b}}), then supp⁡(𝐛)\supp({\mathbf{b}}) and supp⁡(𝐛′)\supp({\mathbf{b}}^{\prime}) are conjugate in WW.

  3. (3)

    If ℓ𝐒±1​(𝐛){\ell_{{\mathbf{S}}^{\pm 1}}}({\mathbf{b}}) is minimal in Conj⁡(𝐛)\conj({\mathbf{b}}), then Bsupp⁡(𝐛)B_{\supp({\mathbf{b}})} is a minimal parabolic subgroup containing 𝐛{\mathbf{b}} (among all parabolic subgroups, not only the standard ones).

Note that point (3) above does not state the uniqueness of a minimal parabolic subgroup since as mentioned above, the question remains open whether the intersection of two parabolic subgroups is parabolic.

In Section 4, we will prove that the existence of a unique minimal parabolic subgroup containing a given element is equivalent to the following conjecture:

Conjecture 0.6.

Let 𝐛∈B{\mathbf{b}}\in B such that ℓ𝐒±1​(𝐛){\ell_{{\mathbf{S}}^{\pm 1}}}({\mathbf{b}}) is minimal in Conj⁡(𝐛)\conj({\mathbf{b}}) and let I=supp⁡(𝐛)I=\supp({\mathbf{b}}), then any 𝐩∈P{\mathbf{p}}\in P which centralises 𝐛{\mathbf{b}} and is such that 𝛑I⁡(𝐩)=1\bpi_{I}({\mathbf{p}})=1 centralises BIB_{I}.

We also obtain a partial result on the conjugacy problem: one can say that we provide a solution to the conjugacy problem for “reducible” elements in Artin groups with SS finite.

Proposition 0.7.

(Propositions 4.17 and 4.18) Assume SS is finite and let Λ\Lambda be a non-empty set of subsets of SS such that for any II in Λ\Lambda, the word problem and the conjugacy problem are solvable in BIB_{I}. Then the two following problems are solvable.

  1. (1)

    Given II in Λ\Lambda and a word bb on 𝐈±1=𝐈∪𝐈−1{\mathbf{I}}^{\pm 1}={\mathbf{I}}\cup{\mathbf{I}}^{-1}, decide whether the word bb represents the unity in BB.

  2. (2)

    Given two finite subsets I,JI,J in Λ\Lambda and words i,ji,j on 𝐈±1{\mathbf{I}}^{\pm 1} and 𝐉±1{\mathbf{J}}^{\pm 1}, respectively, decide whether or not ii and jj represent conjugate elements in BB.

The paper is structured as follows.

In Section 1 we focus on words. If XX is a set, we denote by X∗X^{*} the set of words on XX. Using root systems, we give an alternate definition of the retraction π^I\hpi_{I} from (𝐒±1)∗({\mathbf{S}}^{\pm 1})^{*}, the words on 𝐒∪𝐒−1{\mathbf{S}}\cup{\mathbf{S}}^{-1}, to (𝐒I±1)∗({\mathbf{S}}_{I}^{\pm 1})^{*} and extend some results of [14]. We obtain new results for words in (𝐒±1)∗({\mathbf{S}}^{\pm 1})^{*} whose image in WW is II-reduced-JJ.

In Section 2, we introduce the retraction 𝝅I\bpi_{I} on the Artin group and use the results of the previous section to prove Propositions 0.1 and  0.2. Using the notion of biclosed subset and results of Dyer we study the compatibility of the retraction with lcm’s and gcd’s.

In Section 3 we turn to the projection 𝝅Ir\bpi^{r}_{I} and prove Propositions 0.3 and 0.4.

In Section 4 we consider the conjugacy classes, prove Propositions 0.5, 0.7 and state Conjecture 0.6 .

Finally, we provide in Section 5 (assuming SS finite) a new topological version of 𝝅I\bpi_{I} restricted to pr−1⁡(WI)\pr^{-1}(W_{I}), using the Tits cone and results of Van der Lek [19].

1. Retraction on words

For I⊆SI\subseteq S, we recall that an element w∈Ww\in W is said to be II-reduced (resp. reduced-II) if ℓS​(i​w)=ℓS​(i)+ℓS​(w)\ell_{S}(iw)=\ell_{S}(i)+\ell_{S}(w) (resp. ℓS​(w​i)=ℓS​(i)+ℓS​(w)\ell_{S}(wi)=\ell_{S}(i)+\ell_{S}(w)) for any i∈WIi\in W_{I}, or equivalently for any i∈Ii\in I. We say that an element is II-reduced-JJ if it is both II-reduced and reduced-JJ. For w∈Ww\in W the unique element of minimum length in the coset WI​wW_{I}\,w is II-reduced; we denote it by tI​(w)t_{I}(w).

Lemma 1.1.

If ww is II-reduced and s∈Ss\in S, then the property that sw∈WI\kern 0.5pt\vphantom{s}{}^{w}\kern-0.5pts\in W_{I} is equivalent to w​sws not being II-reduced. Furthermore, in this case sw∈I\kern 0.5pt\vphantom{s}{}^{w}\kern-0.5pts\in I.

Proof.

Assume first that ℓS​(w​s)>ℓS​(w)\ell_{S}(ws)>\ell_{S}(w). If w​sws is not II-reduced, then there exists s′∈Is^{\prime}\in I such that ℓS​(s′​w​s)<ℓS​(w​s)\ell_{S}(s^{\prime}ws)<\ell_{S}(ws), which by the exchange lemma implies that s′​w​ss^{\prime}ws is either equal to ww or to w^​s\hat{w}s where ℓS​(w^)<ℓS​(w)\ell_{S}(\hat{w})<\ell_{S}(w) . But s′​w​s=w^​ss^{\prime}ws=\hat{w}s contradicts the fact that ww is II-reduced, so that s′​w​s=ws^{\prime}ws=w, that is sw=s′∈I\kern 0.5pt\vphantom{s}{}^{w}\kern-0.5pts=s^{\prime}\in I. Conversely if sw∈WI\kern 0.5pt\vphantom{s}{}^{w}\kern-0.5pts\in W_{I} then w​s∈WI​wws\in W_{I}w so is not II-reduced.

Now if ℓS​(w​s)<ℓS​(w)\ell_{S}(ws)<\ell_{S}(w), write w=w′​sw=w^{\prime}s, then w​s=w′ws=w^{\prime} is II-reduced and by the first case ws=w′s\kern 0.5pt\vphantom{s}{}^{w}\kern-0.5pts=\kern 0.5pt\vphantom{s}^{w^{\prime}}\kern-0.5pts is not in WIW_{I}. ∎

Definition 1.2 (Retraction).

Write b∈(𝐒±1)∗b\in({\mathbf{S}}^{\pm 1})^{*} as b=𝐬1ε1​|…|​𝐬kεkb={\mathbf{s}}_{1}^{\varepsilon_{1}}|\ldots|{\mathbf{s}}_{k}^{\varepsilon_{k}} where εi=±1\varepsilon_{i}=\pm 1 and 𝐬i∈𝐒{\mathbf{s}}_{i}\in{\mathbf{S}}. For 1≤j≤k1\leq j\leq k let wj=s1​…​sjw_{j}=s_{1}\ldots s_{j} be the image in WW of the jj first letters of bb. We apply Lemma 1.1 to tI​(wj−1)t_{I}(w_{j-1}) (with w0=1w_{0}=1) to deduce that if x=tI​(wj−1)sj∈WIx=\kern 0.5pt\vphantom{s}^{t_{I}(w_{j-1})}\kern-0.5pts_{j}\in W_{I} then x∈Ix\in I; we denote then xx by sf⁡(j)s_{f(j)} and say that jj is good; otherwise we say that jj is bad and set sf⁡(j)=1s_{f(j)}=1. The retraction π^I⁡(b)\hpi_{I}(b) is the word in (𝐈±1)∗({\mathbf{I}}^{\pm 1})^{*} whose letters are the 𝐬f⁡(j)εj{\mathbf{s}}_{f(j)}^{\varepsilon_{j}} for jj good taken in increasing order.

This definition is equivalent to that in [2, Page 1522] though the notation there makes it a little bit difficult to see.

Remark 1.3.

The following points are clear from the definition.

  1. (1)

    π^I⁡(b)=b\hpi_{I}(b)=b if and only if b∈(𝐈±1)∗b\in({\mathbf{I}}^{\pm 1})^{*}.

  2. (2)

    If the word bb is a prefix of the word b′b^{\prime} then π^I⁡(b)\hpi_{I}(b) is a prefix of π^I⁡(b′)\hpi_{I}(b^{\prime}).

  3. (3)

    π^I\hpi_{I} sends 𝐒∗{\mathbf{S}}^{*} (positive words) to 𝐈∗{\mathbf{I}}^{*}.

  4. (4)

    π^I\hpi_{I} commutes with the map (𝐒±1)∗→(𝐒±1)∗({\mathbf{S}}^{\pm 1})^{*}\to({\mathbf{S}}^{\pm 1})^{*} induced by 𝐬↦𝐬−1{\mathbf{s}}\mapsto{\mathbf{s}}^{-1} for 𝐬∈𝐒±1{\mathbf{s}}\in{\mathbf{S}}^{\pm 1}.

  5. (5)

    We denote by ℓ⁡(b){\ell}(b) the length of b∈(𝐒±1)∗b\in({\mathbf{S}}^{\pm 1})^{*}. For any word bb we have ℓ⁡(π^I⁡(b))≤ℓ⁡(b){\ell}(\hpi_{I}(b))\leq{\ell}(b), with equality if and only if b∈(𝐈±1)∗b\in({\mathbf{I}}^{\pm 1})^{*}.

An efficient way to compute tI​(wj)t_{I}(w_{j}) is given by the following lemma.

Lemma 1.4.

In the setting of Definition 1.2, for 1≤j≤k1\leq j\leq k we have

  1. (1)

    tI​(wj)t_{I}(w_{j}) is equal to the product of the sls_{l} such that ll is bad and 1≤l≤j1\leq l\leq j,

  2. (2)

    tI​(wj−1)​sj=sf⁡(j)​tI​(wj)t_{I}(w_{j-1})s_{j}=s_{f(j)}t_{I}(w_{j}).

  3. (3)

    For all jj, we have wj=sf⁡(1)⋯sf⁡(j)tI(wj)w_{j}=s_{f(1)}\cdots s_{f(j)}t_{I}(w_{j}).

Proof.

We prove items (1) and (2) at the same time by induction on jj. Assume that tI​(wj−1)t_{I}(w_{j-1}) is the product of the sls_{l} for ll bad and l≤j−1l\leq j-1. Lemma 1.5.

We call reflections of WW the WW-conjugates of the elements of SS and denote their set by TT (and similarly denote by TIT_{I} the set of reflections of WIW_{I}).

Lemma 1.13.

Let I,J⊆SI,J\subseteq S and let w∈Ww\in W be II-reduced-JJ; then I1=I∩wJI_{1}=I\cap\kern 0.5pt\vphantom{J}^{w}\kern-0.5ptJ is the unique maximal subset of II such that I1w⊆JI_{1}^{w}\subseteq J. This is clear. ∎

Definition 1.14.

Let I⊆SI\subseteq S; an element w∈Ww\in W which is II-reduced and such that Iw⊆SI^{w}\subseteq S is called an II-ribbon. If J=IwJ=I^{w} we also call it an II-ribbon-JJ or a ribbon-JJ, in order to specify JJ.

In this situation ww is also reduced-JJ and w−1w^{-1} induces a bijection φw:J→∼I\varphi_{w}:J\xrightarrow{\sim}I, which lifts naturally to a bijection from (𝐉±1)∗({\mathbf{J}}^{\pm 1})^{*} to (𝐈±1)∗({\mathbf{I}}^{\pm 1})^{*} that we still denote by φw\varphi_{w}.

Remark 1.15.

Under the assumptions of Lemma 1.13, the element ww is a I1I_{1}-ribbon-J1J_{1}; indeed we have I1w=J1I_{1}^{w}=J_{1} and ww is I1I_{1}-reduced-J1J_{1}. Moreover I1I_{1} and J1J_{1} are the maximal subsets of II and JJ respectively with that property.

Proposition 1.16.

For I,J⊆SI,J\subseteq S, let b,b′∈(𝐒±1)∗b,b^{\prime}\in({\mathbf{S}}^{\pm 1})^{*} be such that pr^⁡(b)\hpr(b) is an II-ribbon-JJ. Then π^I⁡(b|b′)=π^I⁡(b)|φpr^⁡(b)​(π^J⁡(b′))\hpi_{I}(b|b^{\prime})=\hpi_{I}(b)|\varphi_{\hpr(b)}(\hpi_{J}(b^{\prime})).

Proof.

Proposition 1.11 gives π^I(b|b′)=π^I(b)|p∗−1(N→(N→(pr^⁡(b)p∗(b′))∩ΦI))\hpi_{I}(b|b^{\prime})=\hpi_{I}(b)|p^{*-1}(\vec{N}(\vec{N}(\kern 0.5pt\vphantom{p}^{\hpr(b)}\kern-0.5ptp^{*}(b^{\prime}))\cap\Phi_{I})). Using that ΦIpr^⁡(b)=ΦJ\Phi_{I}^{\hpr(b)}=\Phi_{J} the second term of the right-hand side is equal to

p∗−1(pr^⁡(b)N→(N→(p∗(b′))∩ΦJ))=φpr^⁡(b)(p∗−1(N→(N→(p∗(b′))∩ΦJ)))=φpr^⁡(b)(π^J(b′)).p^{*-1}(\kern 0.5pt\vphantom{\vec{N}}^{\hpr(b)}\kern-0.5pt\vec{N}(\vec{N}(p^{*}(b^{\prime}))\cap\Phi_{J}))=\varphi_{\hpr(b)}(p^{*-1}(\vec{N}(\vec{N}(p^{*}(b^{\prime}))\cap\Phi_{J})))=\varphi_{\hpr(b)}(\hpi_{J}(b^{\prime})).

∎

If we lift an expression w=s1⋯skw=s_{1}\cdots s_{k} to a word w^∈𝐒∗\hat{w}\in{\mathbf{S}}^{*}, the image N⁡(w)N(w) in ℤ/2​ℤ​[T]{\mathbb{Z}}/2{\mathbb{Z}}[T] of N→​(p∗​(w^))\vec{N}(p^{*}(\hat{w})), obtained by associating to each root the corresponding reflection, depends only on ww. Indeed N(w)=∑i=1,…,ks1⋯si−1si∈ℤ/2ℤ[T]N(w)=\sum_{i=1,\ldots,k}\kern 0.5pt\vphantom{s}^{s_{1}\cdots s_{i-1}}\kern-0.5pts_{i}\in{\mathbb{Z}}/2{\mathbb{Z}}[T] can also be considered as the subset of TT consisting of elements which appear an odd number of times in the sequence {s1⋯si−1si}1≤i≤k\{\kern 0.5pt\vphantom{s}^{s_{1}\cdots s_{i-1}}\kern-0.5pts_{i}\}_{1\leq i\leq k}; it is known that NN depends only on ww (see [3, Chapter IV, §1.4, Lemme 2]). It is also shown in loc. cit. that NN is injective and that |N​(w)|=ℓS​(w)|N(w)|=\ell_{S}(w). For v,v′∈Wv,v^{\prime}\in W one has N(vv′)=N(v)+vN(v′)N(vv^{\prime})=N(v)+\kern 0.5pt\vphantom{N}^{v}\kern-0.5ptN(v^{\prime}).

The next proposition is [18, Lemma 2]. The proof we give, in the setting of the elementary Coxeter group theory, is shorter that the original proof.

Proposition 1.17.

Let I,JI,J be subsets of SS and w∈Ww\in W be II-reduced-JJ. Then WJ∩WIw=WJ1W_{J}\cap W_{I}^{w}=W_{J_{1}} where J1=Iw∩JJ_{1}=I^{w}\cap J.

Proof.

If y∈WJ∩WIwy\in W_{J}\cap W_{I}^{w} then w​y∈WI​wwy\in W_{I}w so we can write w​y=x​wwy=xw with x∈WIx\in W_{I}. We get thus N⁡(w)​∐wN⁡(y)=N⁡(x)​∐xN⁡(w)N(w)\coprod\kern 0.5pt\vphantom{N}^{w}\kern-0.5ptN(y)=N(x)\coprod\kern 0.5pt\vphantom{N}^{x}\kern-0.5ptN(w) where the sums are disjoint because ww is reduced on both sides. But since ww is II-reduced N⁡(w)N(w) does not meet WIW_{I}, thus N(w)⊆xN(w)N(w)\subseteq\kern 0.5pt\vphantom{N}^{x}\kern-0.5ptN(w) and we must have equality since these sets have same cardinality. Thus in turn we must have Nw​(y)=N​(x)\kern 0.5pt\vphantom{N}{}^{w}\kern-0.5ptN(y)=N(x). We claim that by induction on ℓS​(y)\ell_{S}(y) the assertion Nw​(y)⊆WI\kern 0.5pt\vphantom{N}{}^{w}\kern-0.5ptN(y)\subseteq W_{I} implies y∈WJ1y\in W_{J_{1}}. By Lemma 1.1 the fact that sw∈WI\kern 0.5pt\vphantom{s}{}^{w}\kern-0.5pts\in W_{I} implies sw∈I\kern 0.5pt\vphantom{s}{}^{w}\kern-0.5pts\in I thus s∈J1s\in J_{1}, and w​s=t​wws=tw for some t∈It\in I. Using N⁡(s​y′)=s​∐sN⁡(y′)N(sy^{\prime})=s\coprod\kern 0.5pt\vphantom{N}^{s}\kern-0.5ptN(y^{\prime}) we get Nw​s​(y′)⊆WI\kern 0.5pt\vphantom{N}{}^{ws}\kern-0.5ptN(y^{\prime})\subseteq W_{I}, and since w​s=t​wws=tw this implies Nw​(y′)⊆WI\kern 0.5pt\vphantom{N}{}^{w}\kern-0.5ptN(y^{\prime})\subseteq W_{I} and we conclude by induction. ∎

Corollary 1.18.

Let I,JI,J be subsets of SS and w∈Ww\in W be II-reduced-JJ. Then ΦJ∩ΦIw=ΦJ1\Phi_{J}\cap\Phi_{I}^{w}=\Phi_{J_{1}} where J1=Iw∩JJ_{1}=I^{w}\cap J.

Proposition 1.19.

Let I,J⊆SI,J\subseteq S and b∈(𝐒±1)∗b\in({\mathbf{S}}^{\pm 1})^{*} be such that pr^⁡(b)\hpr(b) is II-reduced-JJ. 2. Retraction on braids

We say that a subgroup of WW is parabolic if it is conjugate to a standard parabolic subgroup of WW.

As a direct application of Proposition 1.17, we get

Lemma 2.1.

the intersection of any two parabolic subgroups DD and QQ of WW is a parabolic subgroup of each of them.

Proof.

Up to conjugacy, we may assume that QQ is standard, say Q=WJQ=W_{J}. Assume D=WIvD=W_{I}^{v}. Write w=i​w​jw=iwj with i∈WIi\in W_{I}, j∈WJj\in W_{J} and ww II-reduced-JJ. Then D∩Q=(WJ∩WIw)vD\cap Q=(W_{J}\cap W_{I}^{w})^{v}, and we conclude by Proposition 1.17. ∎

Lemma 2.2.

For any parabolic subgroups Q,DQ,D of WW where DD is dihedral the set T∩Q∩DT\cap Q\cap D is either empty, or is reduced to one reflection or is the set T∩DT\cap D of all reflections of DD.

Proof.

By Lemma 2.1 the intersection of the two parabolic subgroups DD and QQ of WW is a parabolic subgroup of each of them. The possible parabolic subgroups of DD are {1}\{1\}, a subgroup generated by one reflection, or DD itself. This gives the three cases of the statement. ∎

Lemma 2.3.

Let b,b′∈(𝐒±1)∗b,b^{\prime}\in({\mathbf{S}}^{\pm 1})^{*} and assume one of the following for two words rr and r′r^{\prime} in (𝐒±1)∗({\mathbf{S}}^{\pm 1})^{*}:

  1. (1)

    r,r′r,r^{\prime} are the two members of a braid relation,

  2. (2)

    r=𝐬|𝐬−1r={\mathbf{s}}|{\mathbf{s}}^{-1} or 𝐬−1|𝐬{\mathbf{s}}^{-1}|{\mathbf{s}} and r′r^{\prime} is the empty word,

then the two words π^I⁡(b​|r|​b′)\hpi_{I}(b|r|b^{\prime}) and π^I⁡(b​|r′|​b′)\hpi_{I}(b|r^{\prime}|b^{\prime}) are either equal or differ by a relation in (𝐈±1)∗({\mathbf{I}}^{\pm 1})^{*} of the same type as the relation r≡r′r\equiv r^{\prime}.

Proof.

Applying Corollary 1.12 to b​|r|​b′b|r|b^{\prime} and b​|r′|​b′b|r^{\prime}|b^{\prime}, since pr^⁡(r)=pr^⁡(r′)\hpr(r)=\hpr(r^{\prime}), it is sufficient to compare p∗−1(N→(N→(tI​(pr^⁡(b))p∗(r))∩ΦI))p^{*-1}(\vec{N}(\vec{N}(\kern 0.5pt\vphantom{p}^{t_{I}(\hpr(b))}\kern-0.5ptp^{*}(r))\cap\Phi_{I})) and p∗−1(N→(N→(tI​(pr^⁡(b))p∗(r′))∩ΦI))p^{*-1}(\vec{N}(\vec{N}(\kern 0.5pt\vphantom{p}^{t_{I}(\hpr(b))}\kern-0.5ptp^{*}(r^{\prime}))\cap\Phi_{I})). Using Lemma 1.6(3) it is equivalent to compare for any II-reduced element w∈Ww\in W the words p∗−1(N→(wN→(p∗(r))∩ΦI))p^{*-1}(\vec{N}(\kern 0.5pt\vphantom{\vec{N}}^{w}\kern-0.5pt\vec{N}(p^{*}(r))\cap\Phi_{I})) and p∗−1(N→(wN→(p∗(r′))∩ΦI))p^{*-1}(\vec{N}(\kern 0.5pt\vphantom{\vec{N}}^{w}\kern-0.5pt\vec{N}(p^{*}(r^{\prime}))\cap\Phi_{I})).

In case (1) the sequences in N→​(p∗​(r))\vec{N}(p^{*}(r)) and N→​(p∗​(r′))\vec{N}(p^{*}(r^{\prime})) are reversed from each other and consist of all the positive roots of a standard dihedral parabolic. Hence the roots in N→(p∗(r))∩w−1ΦI\vec{N}(p^{*}(r))\cap\kern 0.5pt\vphantom{\Phi}^{w^{-1}}\kern-0.5pt\Phi_{I} and N→(p∗(r′))∩w−1ΦI\vec{N}(p^{*}(r^{\prime}))\cap\kern 0.5pt\vphantom{\Phi}^{w^{-1}}\kern-0.5pt\Phi_{I} are all the positive roots in the intersection of that dihedral subgroup with WIw−1\kern 0.5pt\vphantom{W}{}^{w^{-1}}\kern-0.5ptW_{I}. By Lemma 2.2 there are three cases for this set of roots: either it is empty or it is reduced to one root or it is the set of all the positive roots of a dihedral parabolic subroup of WIw−1\kern 0.5pt\vphantom{W}{}^{w^{-1}}\kern-0.5ptW_{I}.

In the first two cases we get clearly the equality of the sequences N→(wN→(p∗(r))∩ΦI)\vec{N}(\kern 0.5pt\vphantom{\vec{N}}^{w}\kern-0.5pt\vec{N}(p^{*}(r))\cap\Phi_{I}) and N→(wN→(p∗(r′))∩ΦI)\vec{N}(\kern 0.5pt\vphantom{\vec{N}}^{w}\kern-0.5pt\vec{N}(p^{*}(r^{\prime}))\cap\Phi_{I}). In the third case we have N→(wN→(p∗(r))∩ΦI)=N→(wN→(p∗(r)))=wp∗(r)\vec{N}(\kern 0.5pt\vphantom{\vec{N}}^{w}\kern-0.5pt\vec{N}(p^{*}(r))\cap\Phi_{I})=\vec{N}(\kern 0.5pt\vphantom{\vec{N}}^{w}\kern-0.5pt\vec{N}(p^{*}(r)))=\kern 0.5pt\vphantom{p}^{w}\kern-0.5ptp^{*}(r) and N→(wN→(p∗(r′))∩ΦI)=N→(wN→(p∗(r′)))=wp∗(r′)\vec{N}(\kern 0.5pt\vphantom{\vec{N}}^{w}\kern-0.5pt\vec{N}(p^{*}(r^{\prime}))\cap\Phi_{I})=\vec{N}(\kern 0.5pt\vphantom{\vec{N}}^{w}\kern-0.5pt\vec{N}(p^{*}(r^{\prime})))=\kern 0.5pt\vphantom{p}^{w}\kern-0.5ptp^{*}(r^{\prime}) and these two sequences are reversed from each other and are sequences in ΠI∗\Pi_{I}^{*}. Thus applying p∗−1p^{*-1} gives the two members of a braid relation in BIB_{I}, whence the result.

In case (2) we have N→w​(p∗​(r))=α|−α\kern 0.5pt\vphantom{\vec{N}}{}^{w}\kern-0.5pt\vec{N}(p^{*}(r))=\alpha|-\alpha for some root α\alpha. If α∉ΦI\alpha\notin\Phi_{I}, then OPENN→w​(p∗​(r))∩ΦI)\kern 0.5pt\vphantom{\vec{N}}{}^{w}\kern-0.5pt\vec{N}(p^{*}(r))\cap\Phi_{I}) is the empty sequence and π^I⁡(b​|r|​b′)\hpi_{I}(b|r|b^{\prime}) and π^I⁡(b​|r′|​b′)\hpi_{I}(b|r^{\prime}|b^{\prime}) are equal. If α∈ΦI\alpha\in\Phi_{I} then the two words p∗−1(N→(wN→(p∗(r))∩ΦI))p^{*-1}(\vec{N}(\kern 0.5pt\vphantom{\vec{N}}^{w}\kern-0.5pt\vec{N}(p^{*}(r))\cap\Phi_{I})) and p∗−1(N→(wN→(p∗(r′))∩ΦI))p^{*-1}(\vec{N}(\kern 0.5pt\vphantom{\vec{N}}^{w}\kern-0.5pt\vec{N}(p^{*}(r^{\prime}))\cap\Phi_{I})) differ by a relation of type 𝐬|𝐬−1≡∅{\mathbf{s}}|{\mathbf{s}}^{-1}\equiv\emptyset or 𝐬−1|𝐬≡∅{\mathbf{s}}^{-1}|{\mathbf{s}}\equiv\emptyset with 𝐬∈𝐈{\mathbf{s}}\in{\mathbf{I}}. ∎

Proposition 2.4.

For b∈(𝐒±1)∗b\in({\mathbf{S}}^{\pm 1})^{*} of image 𝐛{\mathbf{b}} in BB, the image in BB of π^I⁡(b)\hpi_{I}(b) depends only on 𝐛{\mathbf{b}}. We call it 𝛑I⁡(𝐛)\bpi_{I}({\mathbf{b}}).

Proof.

This is an immediate consequence of Lemma 2.3. ∎

The following proposition was first proved by Van der Lek. In [19], SS is assumed to be finite but the result for infinite SS is an almost immediate consequence.

Proposition 2.5.

For I⊆SI\subseteq S, the natural morphism from the braid group of WIW_{I} to BIB_{I} is an isomorphism.

Proof.

The morphism is clearly surjective. We show the injectivity. Let bb be a word in (𝐈±1)∗({\mathbf{I}}^{\pm 1})^{*}. We have to show that if b≡∅b\equiv\emptyset in BB, then the same equivalence occurs using only relations in (𝐈±1)∗({\mathbf{I}}^{\pm 1})^{*}. Let b=b1≡b2≡…≡∅b=b_{1}\equiv b_{2}\equiv\ldots\equiv\emptyset be a chain of equivalences in BB by relations of the type considered in Lemma 2.3. Apply π^I\hpi_{I} to this chain. The first and the last term are unchanged, and by Lemma 2.3 each other equivalence is mapped to an equivalence in (𝐈±1)∗({\mathbf{I}}^{\pm 1})^{*}. This proves the result. ∎

Lemma 2.7.

Let 𝐛∈B{\mathbf{b}}\in B be such that pr⁡(𝐛)∈NW​(WI)\pr({\mathbf{b}})\in N_{W}(W_{I}); then there exists a unique w∈Ww\in W such that ww is an II-ribbon-II and such that pr⁡(𝐛)∈WI​w\pr({\mathbf{b}})\in W_{I}w. For any 𝐛′∈B{\mathbf{b}}^{\prime}\in B we have 𝛑I⁡(𝐛𝐛′)=𝛑I⁡(𝐛)​φw​(𝛑I⁡(𝐛′))\bpi_{I}({\mathbf{b}}{\mathbf{b}}^{\prime})=\bpi_{I}({\mathbf{b}})\varphi_{w}(\bpi_{I}({\mathbf{b}}^{\prime})).

Let 𝐰∈𝐖{\mathbf{w}}\in{\mathbf{W}} be the lift of ww and 𝐛1=𝐛𝐰−1{\mathbf{b}}_{1}={\mathbf{b}}{\mathbf{w}}^{-1}; then pr⁡(𝐛1)∈WI\pr({\mathbf{b}}_{1})\in W_{I} and, by items (7) and (8) of Proposition 2.6, we have 𝝅I⁡(𝐛𝐛′)=𝝅I⁡(𝐛1)​𝝅I⁡(𝐰𝐛′)=𝝅I⁡(𝐛1)​φw​(𝝅I⁡(𝐛′))\bpi_{I}({\mathbf{b}}{\mathbf{b}}^{\prime})=\bpi_{I}({\mathbf{b}}_{1})\bpi_{I}({\mathbf{w}}{\mathbf{b}}^{\prime})=\bpi_{I}({\mathbf{b}}_{1})\varphi_{w}(\bpi_{I}({\mathbf{b}}^{\prime})). The following lemma shows that the definitions tI,𝐭it_{I},{\mathbf{t}}_{i} and πI,𝝅I\pi_{I},\bpi_{I} are compatible.

Lemma 2.9.

Let I⊆SI\subseteq S and 𝐛{\mathbf{b}} be in BB.

  1. (1)

    𝝅I⁡(𝐭I​(𝐛))=1\bpi_{I}({\mathbf{t}}_{I}({\mathbf{b}}))=1.

  2. (2)

  4. (4)

    If 𝐛′{\mathbf{b}}^{\prime} is in BB, then BI​𝐛=BI​𝐛′⇔𝐭I​(𝐛)=𝐭I​(𝐛′)B_{I}{\mathbf{b}}=B_{I}{\mathbf{b}}^{\prime}\iff{\mathbf{t}}_{I}({\mathbf{b}})={\mathbf{t}}_{I}({\mathbf{b}}^{\prime}).

Note that (3) can be seen as a part of the commutative diagram in Proposition 2.22.

Proof.

The map 𝐍{\mathbf{N}}

The following proposition is [10, Proposition 2.1]. We recall it here, as it is unpublished.

Proposition 2.18.

a

  1. (1)

    There exists a well defined map 𝐍:B→ℤ⁡[T]{\mathbf{N}}:B\to{\mathbb{Z}}[T] such that

    𝐍(𝐬1ε1⋯𝐬kεk)=∑i=1i=kεis1⋯si−1si{\mathbf{N}}({\mathbf{s}}_{1}^{\varepsilon_{1}}\cdots{\mathbf{s}}_{k}^{\varepsilon_{k}})=\sum_{i=1}^{i=k}\varepsilon_{i}\kern 0.5pt\vphantom{s}^{s_{1}\cdots s_{i-1}}\kern-0.5pts_{i}

    for 𝐬i∈𝐒{\mathbf{s}}_{i}\in{\mathbf{S}} and εi=±1\varepsilon_{i}=\pm 1.

  2. (2)

    The map 𝐍⋊pr{\mathbf{N}}\rtimes\pr is group homomorphism from BB to ℤ⁡[T]⋊W{\mathbb{Z}}[T]\rtimes W, where the action of WW on ℤ⁡[T]{\mathbb{Z}}[T] extends linearly the conjugation action of WW on TT.

Proof.

We prove that the map 𝐬↦(s,s){\mathbf{s}}\mapsto(s,s) for 𝐬∈𝐒{\mathbf{s}}\in{\mathbf{S}} extends to a group morphism f:B→ℤ⁡[T]⋊Wf:B\to{\mathbb{Z}}[T]\rtimes W. Composing this morphism with the first projection will give a map 𝐍{\mathbf{N}} which satisfies (1). It is sufficient to show that the braid relations (∗⁣∗**) are satisfied, that is for any 𝐬,𝐭∈𝐒{\mathbf{s}},{\mathbf{t}}\in{\mathbf{S}}, we have the equality f(𝐬)f(𝐭)⋯=f(𝐭)f(𝐬)⋯f({\mathbf{s}})f({\mathbf{t}})\cdots=f({\mathbf{t}})f({\mathbf{s}})\cdots, where there are ms,tm_{s,t} terms on both sides. In ℤ⁡[T]⋊W{\mathbb{Z}}[T]\rtimes W the first component of (s,s)(t,t)⋯(s,s)(t,t)\cdots (with ms,tm_{s,t} factors) is the sum of all reflections of the dihedral group generated by ss and tt and the second component is the longest element of this dihedral group. So we get the same result by swapping ss and tt, whence the proposition. ∎

The map 𝐍{\mathbf{N}} lifts NN to the braid group: for 𝐛∈B{\mathbf{b}}\in B the set N⁡(pr⁡(𝐛))N(\pr({\mathbf{b}})) is the reduction modulo 2 of 𝐍⁡(𝐛){\mathbf{N}}({\mathbf{b}}). For 𝐰∈𝐖{\mathbf{w}}\in{\mathbf{W}} we can identify 𝐍⁡(𝐰){\mathbf{N}}({\mathbf{w}}) to N⁡(w)N(w): one gets 𝐍⁡(𝐰){\mathbf{N}}({\mathbf{w}}) from N⁡(w)N(w) by lifting ℤ/2​ℤ{\mathbb{Z}}/2{\mathbb{Z}} to {0,1}⊆ℤ\{0,1\}\subseteq{\mathbb{Z}}. If we interpret 𝐍{\mathbf{N}} as a map B→ℤ⁡[Φ+]B\to{\mathbb{Z}}[\Phi^{+}], then 𝐍⁡(𝐛){\mathbf{N}}({\mathbf{b}}) is the sum of the sequence N→​(p∗​(b))\vec{N}(p^{*}(b)) for any word bb representing 𝐛{\mathbf{b}}.

Lemma 2.19.

We say that 𝐰∈𝐖{\mathbf{w}}\in{\mathbf{W}} is II-reduced if pr⁡(𝐰)\pr({\mathbf{w}}) is II-reduced.

    The pure braid group PP is generated by PI=P∩BIP_{I}=P\cap B_{I} and the elements 𝐢𝐰𝐬2​𝐰−1​𝐢−1{\mathbf{i}}{\mathbf{w}}{\mathbf{s}}^{2}{\mathbf{w}}^{-1}{\mathbf{i}}^{-1} for 𝐬∈𝐒{\mathbf{s}}\in{\mathbf{S}} and 𝐢∈𝐖I{\mathbf{i}}\in{\mathbf{W}}_{I} and 𝐰∈𝐖{\mathbf{w}}\in{\mathbf{W}} such that 𝐰𝐬{\mathbf{w}}{\mathbf{s}} is an II-reduced element.

Proof.

We first prove that PP is generated by the 𝐰𝐬𝐰−1{\mathbf{w}}{\mathbf{s}}{\mathbf{w}}^{-1} with 𝐰,𝐬,𝐰𝐬∈𝐖{\mathbf{w}},{\mathbf{s}},{\mathbf{w}}{\mathbf{s}}\in{\mathbf{W}}: if in the Reidemeister-Shreier method we take 𝐖{\mathbf{W}} as representatives of the PP-cosets in BB, we get that PP is generated by the 𝐰𝐬𝐯−1{\mathbf{w}}{\mathbf{s}}{\mathbf{v}}^{-1} where 𝐰∈𝐖{\mathbf{w}}\in{\mathbf{W}} and 𝐬∈𝐒{\mathbf{s}}\in{\mathbf{S}} and 𝐯∈𝐖{\mathbf{v}}\in{\mathbf{W}} is the representative of 𝐰𝐬{\mathbf{w}}{\mathbf{s}}; if 𝐰𝐬{\mathbf{w}}{\mathbf{s}} is in 𝐖{\mathbf{W}} we have 𝐯=𝐰{\mathbf{v}}={\mathbf{w}}, otherwise 𝐰=𝐮𝐬{\mathbf{w}}={\mathbf{u}}{\mathbf{s}} for some 𝐮∈𝐖{\mathbf{u}}\in{\mathbf{W}} and 𝐯=𝐮{\mathbf{v}}={\mathbf{u}} so that 𝐰𝐬𝐯−1=𝐮𝐬𝐮−1{\mathbf{w}}{\mathbf{s}}{\mathbf{v}}^{-1}={\mathbf{u}}{\mathbf{s}}{\mathbf{u}}^{-1}. We get then the first item of the lemma by writing 𝐰=𝐢𝐯{\mathbf{w}}={\mathbf{i}}{\mathbf{v}} where 𝐢∈𝐖I{\mathbf{i}}\in{\mathbf{W}}_{I} and 𝐯{\mathbf{v}} is II-reduced.

We get the second item from the first using that an element of pr−1⁡(WI)\pr^{-1}(W_{I}) is the product of an element of BIB_{I} by a pure braid.

For the third item, by Proposition 2.6(7) we have 𝝅I⁡(𝐰𝐬2​𝐰−1)​𝝅I⁡(𝐰𝐬−1)=𝝅I⁡(𝐰𝐬)\bpi_{I}({\mathbf{w}}{\mathbf{s}}^{2}{\mathbf{w}}^{-1})\bpi_{I}({\mathbf{w}}{\mathbf{s}}^{-1})=\bpi_{I}({\mathbf{w}}{\mathbf{s}}), and by Proposition 2.6(5) we obtain 𝝅I⁡(𝐰𝐬−1)=𝝅I⁡(𝐰𝐬)=1\bpi_{I}({\mathbf{w}}{\mathbf{s}}^{-1})=\bpi_{I}({\mathbf{w}}{\mathbf{s}})=1. Thus, 𝝅I⁡(𝐰𝐬2​𝐰−1)=1\bpi_{I}({\mathbf{w}}{\mathbf{s}}^{2}{\mathbf{w}}^{-1})=1. ∎

The following diagram is commutative:

Closed subsets

For w∈Ww\in W the set N⁡(w)N(w) is in bijection with the set Φw={α∈Φ+∣w−1​(α)∉Φ+}\Phi_{w}=\{\alpha\in\Phi^{+}\mid w^{-1}(\alpha)\notin\Phi^{+}\} since N⁡(w)={sα∣α∈Φw}N(w)=\{s_{\alpha}\mid\alpha\in\Phi_{w}\}. We now recall results of [12]. We say that a set Γ⊆Φ+\Gamma\subseteq\Phi^{+} is closed if for any α,β∈Γ\alpha,\beta\in\Gamma and a,b∈ℝ>0a,b\in{\mathbb{R}}_{>0}, if a​α+b​β∈Φa\alpha+b\beta\in\Phi then a​α+b​β∈Γa\alpha+b\beta\in\Gamma. We call closure of Γ\Gamma, denoted by Γ¯\overline{\Gamma}, the smallest closed set containing Γ\Gamma. We say that Γ\Gamma is biclosed if it is closed and its complement ∁​Γ\complement\Gamma in Φ+\Phi^{+} is closed. Thanks to the bijection between reflections and positive roots we can use the same words for subsets A⊆TA\subseteq T (closed, notation A¯\bar{A} for the closure, biclosed and notation ∁​A\complement A for the complement in TT). The notion of closed for a set A⊆TA\subseteq T can be given in purely group-theoretic terms: a set AA is closed if and only if given any two reflections s,s′∈Ws,s^{\prime}\in W, the intersection of AA with the dihedral group ⟨s,s′⟩\langle s,s^{\prime}\rangle is closed. In a dihedral group W=⟨s,s′⟩W=\langle s,s^{\prime}\rangle, the group theoretic definition of closed is as follows: we give a total order on TT by s<s​s′​s<s​s′​s​s′​s<…<s′​s​s′<s′s<ss^{\prime}s<ss^{\prime}ss^{\prime}s<\ldots<s^{\prime}ss^{\prime}<s^{\prime} (exchanging ss and s′s^{\prime} gives the opposite order); then a set AA is closed if and only if whenever it contains t,t′∈Tt,t^{\prime}\in T with t<t′t<t^{\prime} it contains any t′′t^{\prime\prime} such that t<t′′<t′t<t^{\prime\prime}<t^{\prime} (see [13, (2.2)] for the equivalence of the group-theoretic condition with closed assuming the existence of a reflection order and see [13, Proposition 2.3] for the existence of a reflection order).

Lemma 2.23.

For 𝐰,𝐰′∈𝐖{\mathbf{w}},{\mathbf{w}}^{\prime}\in{\mathbf{W}} it is equivalent that 𝐰{\mathbf{w}} left-divides 𝐰′{\mathbf{w}}^{\prime} in the monoid B+B^{+} or that N⁡(w)⊆N⁡(w′)N(w)\subseteq N(w^{\prime}).

Proof.

The assumption that 𝐰{\mathbf{w}} left-divides 𝐰′{\mathbf{w}}^{\prime} is equivalent in WW to the existence of v∈Wv\in W such that w′=w​vw^{\prime}=wv and ℓS​(w)+ℓS​(v)=ℓS​(w′)\ell_{S}(w)+\ell_{S}(v)=\ell_{S}(w^{\prime}). By the formula N(wv)=N(w)∪wN(v)N(wv)=N(w)\cup\kern 0.5pt\vphantom{N}^{w}\kern-0.5ptN(v) it is clear that left-divisibility implies N⁡(w)⊆N⁡(w′)N(w)\subseteq N(w^{\prime}). It follows that 𝐬{\mathbf{s}} is also a left-divisor of 𝐰′{\mathbf{w}}^{\prime}. Let w=s​w1w=sw_{1} and w′=s​w1′w^{\prime}=sw^{\prime}_{1}. The following proposition shows various reductions of the problem of the intersection of two parabolic subgroups BJ𝐛\kern 0.5pt\vphantom{B}{}^{{\mathbf{b}}}\kern-0.5ptB_{J} and BIB_{I}. Proposition 3.12.

Let I,JI,J be subsets of SS and 𝐛∈B{\mathbf{b}}\in B.

4. Minimal length elements in a conjugacy class

In this section, we first recall a result on elements of B+B^{+} (Proposition 4.5) which is an important step in proving that in spherical type Artin groups there is a unique minimal parabolic subgroup containing a given element (see [7, Introduction of section 6]). We then show that a conjecture (Conjecture 4.14) which generalises Proposition 4.5 to all conjugacy classes is equivalent in all Artin groups to the existence of a unique minimal parabolic subgroup containing a given element. We conclude with a partial result (Proposition 4.17) on conjugacy.

Positive elements

The goal of this subsection is to introduce the concepts and results on elements of B+B^{+} needed, ending with a proof of Proposition 4.5.

For I⊆SI\subseteq S and 𝐛∈B+{\mathbf{b}}\in B^{+} we define HI​(𝐛)H_{I}({\mathbf{b}}) as the longest prefix of 𝐛{\mathbf{b}} in BI+B^{+}_{I}; we say that an element 𝐠∈B+{\mathbf{g}}\in B^{+} is II-reduced if HI​(𝐠)=1H_{I}({\mathbf{g}})=1. We say that an element 𝐠∈B+{\mathbf{g}}\in B^{+} is an II-ribbon if it is II-reduced and 𝐈𝐠⊆B+{\mathbf{I}}^{\mathbf{g}}\subseteq B^{+}. Since ℓℤ{\ell_{{\mathbb{Z}}}} is constant on a conjugacy class, this is seen to be equivalent to 𝐈𝐠⊆𝐒{\mathbf{I}}^{\mathbf{g}}\subseteq{\mathbf{S}}. For 𝐛∈B+{\mathbf{b}}\in B^{+} we define the support supp⁡(𝐛)\supp({\mathbf{b}}) as the smallest subset I⊆SI\subseteq S such that 𝐛∈BI+{\mathbf{b}}\in B_{I}^{+}. This is well defined since the two sides of a braid relation involve the same elements of 𝐒{\mathbf{S}}. Note that the notions of II-reduced element and of II-ribbon in B+B^{+} are coherent with the corresponding definitions in WW introduced in Section 1: the element 𝐰{\mathbf{w}} in 𝐖{\mathbf{W}} is II-reduced (resp. a II-ribbon) if and only if pr⁡(𝐰)\pr({\mathbf{w}}) is. This is not true if 𝐰∉𝐖{\mathbf{w}}\notin{\mathbf{W}}. For instance 𝐬2{\mathbf{s}}^{2} is not {s}\{s\}-reduced but pr⁡(𝐬)\pr({\mathbf{s}}) is, and is even an {s}\{s\}-ribbon. If 𝐬{\mathbf{s}} and 𝐭{\mathbf{t}} do not commute, then 𝐬2​𝐭{\mathbf{s}}^{2}{\mathbf{t}} is {t}\{t\}-reduced but pr⁡(𝐬2​𝐭)=t\pr({\mathbf{s}}^{2}{\mathbf{t}})=t is not.

Recall that the Garside normal form has been introduced in Section 2. For 𝐛∈B+{\mathbf{b}}\in B^{+} we denote by head⁡(𝐛)\head({\mathbf{b}}) the first term of the Garside normal form of 𝐛{\mathbf{b}} and define tail⁡(𝐛)=head⁡(𝐛)−1​𝐛\tail({\mathbf{b}})=\head({\mathbf{b}})^{-1}{\mathbf{b}}.

Lemma 4.1.

a

  1. (1)

    For 𝐛,𝐠∈B+{\mathbf{b}},{\mathbf{g}}\in B^{+}, if 𝐛𝐠∈B+{\mathbf{b}}^{\mathbf{g}}\in B^{+} then 𝐛head⁡(𝐠)∈B+{\mathbf{b}}^{\head({\mathbf{g}})}\in B^{+}

  2. (2)

    If 𝐠∈B+{\mathbf{g}}\in B^{+} is an II-ribbon, then head⁡(𝐠)\head({\mathbf{g}}) is an II-ribbon.

  3. (3)

    If 𝐠∈B+{\mathbf{g}}\in B^{+} is an II-ribbon, then pr⁡(𝐠)\pr({\mathbf{g}}) is an II-ribbon.

Proof.

For (1), the assumption 𝐛𝐠∈B+{\mathbf{b}}^{\mathbf{g}}\in B^{+} is equivalent to 𝐠{\mathbf{g}} left-dividing 𝐛𝐠{\mathbf{b}}{\mathbf{g}} from which it follows that head⁡(𝐠)\head({\mathbf{g}}) left-divides head⁡(𝐛𝐠)=head⁡(𝐛​head⁡(𝐠))\head({\mathbf{b}}{\mathbf{g}})=\head({\mathbf{b}}\head({\mathbf{g}})), in particular head⁡(𝐠)\head({\mathbf{g}}) left-divides 𝐛​head⁡(𝐠){\mathbf{b}}\head({\mathbf{g}}), that is 𝐛head⁡(𝐠)∈B+{\mathbf{b}}^{\head({\mathbf{g}})}\in B^{+}.

For (2), by (1) we get 𝐈head⁡(𝐠)⊆B+{\mathbf{I}}^{\head({\mathbf{g}})}\subseteq B^{+}. And clearly if 𝐠{\mathbf{g}} is II-reduced then head⁡(𝐠)\head({\mathbf{g}}) also.

Finally (3) is clear if 𝐠∈𝐖{\mathbf{g}}\in{\mathbf{W}} and the general case follows from (2) by induction on the number of terms in the Garside normal form of 𝐠{\mathbf{g}}. ∎

Lemma 4.2.

Let 𝐠∈B+{\mathbf{g}}\in B^{+} be an II-ribbon and let 𝐡∈B+{\mathbf{h}}\in B^{+}. Then HI​(𝐠𝐡)𝐠=HIpr⁡(𝐠)​(𝐡)H_{I}({\mathbf{g}}{\mathbf{h}})^{\mathbf{g}}=H_{I^{\pr({\mathbf{g}})}}({\mathbf{h}}) and HI​(𝐠𝐡)−1​𝐠𝐡=𝐠​HIpr⁡(𝐠)​(𝐡)−1​𝐡H_{I}({\mathbf{g}}{\mathbf{h}})^{-1}{\mathbf{g}}{\mathbf{h}}={\mathbf{g}}H_{I^{\pr({\mathbf{g}})}}({\mathbf{h}})^{-1}{\mathbf{h}}.

Proof.

Let 𝐬∈𝐈{\mathbf{s}}\in{\mathbf{I}} and set 𝐬′=𝐬𝐠{\mathbf{s}}^{\prime}={\mathbf{s}}^{\mathbf{g}}. Both formulae clearly follow if we show that it is equivalent that 𝐬{\mathbf{s}} left-divides 𝐠𝐡{\mathbf{g}}{\mathbf{h}} or that 𝐬′{\mathbf{s}}^{\prime} left-divides 𝐡{\mathbf{h}}.

Now from 𝐬𝐠=𝐠𝐬′{\mathbf{s}}{\mathbf{g}}={\mathbf{g}}{\mathbf{s}}^{\prime} it follows that the right-lcm of 𝐬{\mathbf{s}} and 𝐠{\mathbf{g}} divides 𝐬𝐠{\mathbf{s}}{\mathbf{g}}, thus it must be equal to 𝐬𝐠{\mathbf{s}}{\mathbf{g}}, because ℓℤ​(right-lcm⁡(𝐬,𝐠)){\ell_{{\mathbb{Z}}}}(\rightlcm({\mathbf{s}},{\mathbf{g}})) is at least ℓℤ​(𝐠)+1=ℓℤ​(𝐬𝐠){\ell_{{\mathbb{Z}}}}({\mathbf{g}})+1={\ell_{{\mathbb{Z}}}}({\mathbf{s}}{\mathbf{g}}). Thus 𝐬{\mathbf{s}} left-dividing 𝐠𝐡{\mathbf{g}}{\mathbf{h}} is equivalent to 𝐬𝐠{\mathbf{s}}{\mathbf{g}} left-dividing 𝐠𝐡{\mathbf{g}}{\mathbf{h}} or equivalently to 𝐠𝐬′{\mathbf{g}}{\mathbf{s}}^{\prime} left-dividing 𝐠𝐡{\mathbf{g}}{\mathbf{h}}, which is finally equivalent to 𝐬′{\mathbf{s}}^{\prime} left-dividing 𝐡{\mathbf{h}}. ∎

Proposition 4.3.

Let 𝐠,𝐛∈B+{\mathbf{g}},{\mathbf{b}}\in B^{+} be such that 𝐠{\mathbf{g}} is supp⁡(𝐛)\supp({\mathbf{b}})-reduced and such that 𝐛𝐠∈B+{\mathbf{b}}^{\mathbf{g}}\in B^{+}. Then 𝐠{\mathbf{g}} is a supp⁡(𝐛)\supp({\mathbf{b}})-ribbon and we have supp⁡(𝐛𝐠)=supp⁡(𝐛)pr⁡(𝐠)\supp({\mathbf{b}}^{\mathbf{g}})=\supp({\mathbf{b}})^{\pr({\mathbf{g}})}.

Proof.

We first show that we can reduce to the case where 𝐠{\mathbf{g}} is simple, by arguing by induction on the number of terms of the Garside normal form of 𝐠{\mathbf{g}}.

By Lemma 4.1(1) we have 𝐛head⁡(𝐠)∈B+{\mathbf{b}}^{\head({\mathbf{g}})}\in B^{+}; and for 𝐠{\mathbf{g}} to be supp⁡(𝐛)\supp({\mathbf{b}})-reduced, we certainly need head⁡(𝐠)\head({\mathbf{g}}) to be supp⁡(𝐛)\supp({\mathbf{b}})-reduced.

If we know the theorem in the case where 𝐠{\mathbf{g}} is simple, it follows that the set 𝐉=𝐈head⁡(𝐠){\mathbf{J}}={\mathbf{I}}^{\head({\mathbf{g}})}, where I=supp⁡(𝐛)I=\supp({\mathbf{b}}), is a subset of 𝐒{\mathbf{S}}; and thus 𝐛head⁡(𝐠){\mathbf{b}}^{\head({\mathbf{g}})} has support JJ. We also have that tail⁡(𝐠)\tail({\mathbf{g}}) is JJ-reduced by Lemma 4.2 applied with head⁡(𝐠)\head({\mathbf{g}}) for 𝐠{\mathbf{g}} and tail⁡(𝐠)\tail({\mathbf{g}}) for 𝐡{\mathbf{h}}. Since (𝐛head⁡(𝐠))tail⁡(𝐠)∈B+({\mathbf{b}}^{\head({\mathbf{g}})})^{\tail({\mathbf{g}})}\in B^{+}, we conclude by induction on the number of terms of the normal form of 𝐠{\mathbf{g}} that 𝐉tail⁡(𝐠)⊆𝐒{\mathbf{J}}^{\tail({\mathbf{g}})}\subseteq{\mathbf{S}}, whence the result since 𝐉tail⁡(𝐠)=𝐈𝐠{\mathbf{J}}^{\tail({\mathbf{g}})}={\mathbf{I}}^{\mathbf{g}}.

We now show the theorem when 𝐠{\mathbf{g}} is simple. We write the condition 𝐛𝐠∈B+{\mathbf{b}}^{\mathbf{g}}\in B^{+} as 𝐛𝐠=𝐠𝐮{\mathbf{b}}{\mathbf{g}}={\mathbf{g}}{\mathbf{u}} with 𝐮∈B+{\mathbf{u}}\in B^{+}.

We proceed by an induction on ℓℤ​(𝐛){\ell_{{\mathbb{Z}}}}({\mathbf{b}}). For 𝐬∈𝐒{\mathbf{s}}\in{\mathbf{S}} dividing 𝐛{\mathbf{b}}, we write 𝐛=𝐬𝐛′{\mathbf{b}}={\mathbf{s}}{\mathbf{b}}^{\prime}. We have that 𝐬{\mathbf{s}} left-divides 𝐛𝐠=𝐠𝐮{\mathbf{b}}{\mathbf{g}}={\mathbf{g}}{\mathbf{u}}.

To go on we need the following lemma.

Lemma 4.4.

Let 𝐠∈B+{\mathbf{g}}\in B^{+} be simple and let 𝐬∈𝐒{\mathbf{s}}\in{\mathbf{S}}, 𝐮∈B+{\mathbf{u}}\in B^{+} be such that 𝐬{\mathbf{s}} does not divide 𝐠{\mathbf{g}} but 𝐬{\mathbf{s}} divides 𝐠𝐮{\mathbf{g}}{\mathbf{u}}. Then we have 𝐮=𝐮′​𝐭𝐮′′{\mathbf{u}}={\mathbf{u}}^{\prime}{\mathbf{t}}{\mathbf{u}}^{\prime\prime} where 𝐭∈𝐒{\mathbf{t}}\in{\mathbf{S}}, 𝐮′,𝐮′′∈B+{\mathbf{u}}^{\prime},{\mathbf{u}}^{\prime\prime}\in B^{+} are such that 𝐬𝐠𝐮′=𝐠𝐮′​𝐭{\mathbf{s}}{\mathbf{g}}{\mathbf{u}}^{\prime}={\mathbf{g}}{\mathbf{u}}^{\prime}{\mathbf{t}} is simple.

Proof.

First note that 𝐬{\mathbf{s}} left-divides head⁡(𝐠𝐮)\head({\mathbf{g}}{\mathbf{u}}). Let 𝐠𝐮1=head⁡(𝐠𝐮){\mathbf{g}}{\mathbf{u}}_{1}=\head({\mathbf{g}}{\mathbf{u}}). Since in WW we have ℓS​(s​g​u1)<ℓS​(g​u1)\ell_{S}(sgu_{1})<\ell_{S}(gu_{1}) and ℓS​(s​g)>ℓS​(g)\ell_{S}(sg)>\ell_{S}(g) (in other words the reflection ss is in the left descent set of g​u1gu_{1} but not in that of gg), we have by the exchange lemma g​u1=g​u′​t​u2gu_{1}=gu^{\prime}tu_{2} where t∈St\in S and s​g​u′=g​u′​tsgu^{\prime}=gu^{\prime}t. Lifting back to B+B^{+} we get the lemma with 𝐮′′=𝐮2​tail⁡(𝐠𝐮){\mathbf{u}}^{\prime\prime}={\mathbf{u}}_{2}\tail({\mathbf{g}}{\mathbf{u}}). ∎

We now resume the proof of the proposition. Since 𝐬{\mathbf{s}} does not divide 𝐠{\mathbf{g}}, the lemma gives 𝐮=𝐮′​𝐭𝐮′′{\mathbf{u}}={\mathbf{u}}^{\prime}{\mathbf{t}}{\mathbf{u}}^{\prime\prime} with 𝐭∈𝐒{\mathbf{t}}\in{\mathbf{S}} and 𝐬𝐠𝐮′=𝐠𝐮′​𝐭∈𝐖{\mathbf{s}}{\mathbf{g}}{\mathbf{u}}^{\prime}={\mathbf{g}}{\mathbf{u}}^{\prime}{\mathbf{t}}\in{\mathbf{W}}. From 𝐛𝐠=𝐬𝐛′​𝐠=𝐠𝐮=𝐠𝐮′​𝐭𝐮′′=𝐬𝐠𝐮′​𝐮′′{\mathbf{b}}{\mathbf{g}}={\mathbf{s}}{\mathbf{b}}^{\prime}{\mathbf{g}}={\mathbf{g}}{\mathbf{u}}={\mathbf{g}}{\mathbf{u}}^{\prime}{\mathbf{t}}{\mathbf{u}}^{\prime\prime}={\mathbf{s}}{\mathbf{g}}{\mathbf{u}}^{\prime}{\mathbf{u}}^{\prime\prime} we deduce 𝐛′​𝐠=𝐠𝐮′​𝐮′′{\mathbf{b}}^{\prime}{\mathbf{g}}={\mathbf{g}}{\mathbf{u}}^{\prime}{\mathbf{u}}^{\prime\prime}. Thus 𝐛′,𝐠{\mathbf{b}}^{\prime},{\mathbf{g}} satisfy the assumptions of the theorem, thus by induction on ℓℤ​(𝐛){\ell_{{\mathbb{Z}}}}({\mathbf{b}}) we have 𝐊𝐠⊆𝐒{\mathbf{K}}^{\mathbf{g}}\subseteq{\mathbf{S}} where K=supp⁡(𝐛′)K=\supp({\mathbf{b}}^{\prime}). We still have to prove that 𝐬𝐠∈𝐒{\mathbf{s}}^{\mathbf{g}}\in{\mathbf{S}}. This is already proven unless 𝐬∉𝐊{\mathbf{s}}\not\in{\mathbf{K}}, which we assume now.

We write 𝐛′​𝐠=𝐠𝐛′′{\mathbf{b}}^{\prime}{\mathbf{g}}={\mathbf{g}}{\mathbf{b}}^{\prime\prime} for some 𝐛′′∈B{\mathbf{b}}^{\prime\prime}\in B. Since 𝐬𝐠𝐛′′=𝐠𝐮=𝐠𝐮′​𝐭𝐮′′=𝐬𝐠𝐮′​𝐮′′{\mathbf{s}}{\mathbf{g}}{\mathbf{b}}^{\prime\prime}={\mathbf{g}}{\mathbf{u}}={\mathbf{g}}{\mathbf{u}}^{\prime}{\mathbf{t}}{\mathbf{u}}^{\prime\prime}={\mathbf{s}}{\mathbf{g}}{\mathbf{u}}^{\prime}{\mathbf{u}}^{\prime\prime}, we have 𝐛′′=𝐮′​𝐮′′∈B+{\mathbf{b}}^{\prime\prime}={\mathbf{u}}^{\prime}{\mathbf{u}}^{\prime\prime}\in B^{+}. Now 𝐠𝐲𝐠−1∈𝐊{\mathbf{g}}{\mathbf{y}}{\mathbf{g}}^{-1}\in{\mathbf{K}}, for any y∈supp⁡(𝐛′′)y\in\supp({\mathbf{b}}^{\prime\prime}) hence the element 𝐯=𝐠𝐮′​𝐠−1{\mathbf{v}}={\mathbf{g}}{\mathbf{u}}^{\prime}{\mathbf{g}}^{-1} is in BK+B^{+}_{K}. Proposition 4.5.

Let I⊆SI\subseteq S and let 𝐩∈B+{\mathbf{p}}\in B^{+} be a pure element such that HI​(𝐩)=1H_{I}({\mathbf{p}})=1; if 𝐩{\mathbf{p}} commutes with an element in B+B^{+} of support II then 𝐩{\mathbf{p}} centralises BIB_{I}.

Let 𝐢∈B+{\mathbf{i}}\in B^{+} have support II. By Proposition 4.3 conjugating by 𝐩{\mathbf{p}} maps 𝐈{\mathbf{I}} into 𝐒{\mathbf{S}}. Since 𝐩{\mathbf{p}} is pure applying pr\pr to the equality 𝐩𝐬=𝐬′​𝐩{\mathbf{p}}{\mathbf{s}}={\mathbf{s}}^{\prime}{\mathbf{p}} with 𝐬∈𝐈,𝐬′∈𝐒{\mathbf{s}}\in{\mathbf{I}},{\mathbf{s}}^{\prime}\in{\mathbf{S}} we get pr⁡(𝐬)=pr⁡(𝐬′)\pr({\mathbf{s}})=\pr({\mathbf{s}}^{\prime}) hence 𝐬=𝐬′{\mathbf{s}}={\mathbf{s}}^{\prime}. ∎

General elements

Recall that in the introduction we have defined ℓ𝐒±1:B→ℕ{\ell_{{\mathbf{S}}^{\pm 1}}}:B\to{\mathbb{N}} to be the length function on BB with respect to the generating set 𝐒±1{\mathbf{S}}^{\pm 1}. For 𝐛∈B{\mathbf{b}}\in B, it is equal to ℓ⁡(b){\ell}(b), the length of a minimal word b∈(𝐒±1)∗b\in({\mathbf{S}}^{\pm 1})^{*} representing 𝐛{\mathbf{b}}.

Definition 4.6.

For a word b∈(𝐒±1)∗b\in({\mathbf{S}}^{\pm 1})^{*}, we call supp⁡(b)\supp(b) the minimal subset I⊆SI\subseteq S such that b∈(𝐈±1)∗b\in({\mathbf{I}}^{\pm 1})^{*}.

The following proposition, which enables the definition of support for all elements, is the convexity theorem of Charney and Paris [5, Theorem 1.2].

Proposition 4.7.

For 𝐛∈B{\mathbf{b}}\in B, the set supp⁡(b)\supp(b) is independent of the word bb of shortest length representing 𝐛{\mathbf{b}}. We call it support of 𝐛{\mathbf{b}}, denoted by supp⁡(𝐛)\supp({\mathbf{b}}). For any word b′b^{\prime} representing 𝐛{\mathbf{b}} we have supp⁡(b′)⊇supp⁡(𝐛)\supp(b^{\prime})\supseteq\supp({\mathbf{b}}).

Note that the definition of support for elements of BB is compatible with that given above Lemma 4.1 for elements of B+B^{+}.

Proof.

Let bb be a word of minimal length for 𝐛{\mathbf{b}} and let JJ be the support of a word b′b^{\prime} for 𝐛{\mathbf{b}}. Since π^J⁡(b)\hpi_{J}(b) represents 𝐛{\mathbf{b}}, by minimality we have ℓ⁡(π^J⁡(b))=ℓ⁡(b){\ell}(\hpi_{J}(b))={\ell}(b), whence by Remark 1.3(5), supp⁡(b)⊆J\supp(b)\subseteq J, which proves the proposition. ∎

We denote by Conj⁡(𝐛)\conj({\mathbf{b}}) the conjugacy class of 𝐛{\mathbf{b}} in BB, or ConjB⁡(𝐛)\conj_{B}({\mathbf{b}}) when we want to specify BB.

Proposition 4.12.

Let 𝐛∈B{\mathbf{b}}\in B be such that ℓ𝐒±1​(𝐛){\ell_{{\mathbf{S}}^{\pm 1}}}({\mathbf{b}}) is minimal in Conj⁡(𝐛)\conj({\mathbf{b}}). Then Bsupp⁡(𝐛)B_{\supp({\mathbf{b}})} is a minimal parabolic subgroup containing 𝐛{\mathbf{b}}, and any minimal parabolic subgroup containing 𝐛{\mathbf{b}} is of the form Bsupp⁡(𝐛)𝐩\kern 0.5pt\vphantom{B}{}^{{\mathbf{p}}}\kern-0.5ptB_{\supp({\mathbf{b}})} for some element 𝐩{\mathbf{p}} in CP​(𝐛)C_{P}({\mathbf{b}}) such that 𝛑supp⁡(𝐛)⁡(𝐩)=1\bpi_{\supp({\mathbf{b}})}({\mathbf{p}})=1.

Proof.

We first observe that any minimal parabolic subgroup containing 𝐛{\mathbf{b}} is of the form BI𝐠\kern 0.5pt\vphantom{B}{}^{{\mathbf{g}}}\kern-0.5ptB_{I} with ℓ𝐒±1​(𝐛𝐠)=ℓ𝐒±1​(𝐛){\ell_{{\mathbf{S}}^{\pm 1}}}({\mathbf{b}}^{\mathbf{g}})={\ell_{{\mathbf{S}}^{\pm 1}}}({\mathbf{b}}) and supp⁡(𝐛𝐠)=I\supp({\mathbf{b}}^{\mathbf{g}})=I. Indeed if BI𝐠\kern 0.5pt\vphantom{B}{}^{{\mathbf{g}}}\kern-0.5ptB_{I} is minimal containing 𝐛{\mathbf{b}} then we apply by Proposition 4.10 with 𝐠−1{\mathbf{g}}^{-1} for 𝐠{\mathbf{g}} and 𝐛𝐠{\mathbf{b}}^{\mathbf{g}} for 𝐢{\mathbf{i}}. This shows that up to replacing 𝐠{\mathbf{g}} by 𝐠​𝝅I​(𝐠−1){\mathbf{g}}\bpi_{I}({\mathbf{g}}^{-1}) we may assume that ℓ𝐒±1​(𝐛𝐠)=ℓ𝐒±1​(𝐛){\ell_{{\mathbf{S}}^{\pm 1}}}({\mathbf{b}}^{\mathbf{g}})={\ell_{{\mathbf{S}}^{\pm 1}}}({\mathbf{b}}); and we certainly have supp⁡(𝐛𝐠)=I\supp({\mathbf{b}}^{\mathbf{g}})=I otherwise the proper parabolic subgroup Bsupp⁡(𝐛𝐠)B_{\supp({\mathbf{b}}^{\mathbf{g}})} of BIB_{I} would contain 𝐛𝐠{\mathbf{b}}^{\mathbf{g}} and BI𝐠\kern 0.5pt\vphantom{B}{}^{{\mathbf{g}}}\kern-0.5ptB_{I} would not be minimal containing 𝐛{\mathbf{b}}.

Let now BI𝐠\kern 0.5pt\vphantom{B}{}^{{\mathbf{g}}}\kern-0.5ptB_{I} be any minimal parabolic subgroup containing 𝐛{\mathbf{b}}. We may assume that ℓ𝐒±1​(𝐛𝐠)=ℓ𝐒±1​(𝐛){\ell_{{\mathbf{S}}^{\pm 1}}}({\mathbf{b}}^{\mathbf{g}})={\ell_{{\mathbf{S}}^{\pm 1}}}({\mathbf{b}}) and that supp⁡(𝐛𝐠)=I\supp({\mathbf{b}}^{\mathbf{g}})=I. It follows by Corollary 4.9(1) that supp⁡(𝐛)\supp({\mathbf{b}}) is conjugate to II. So, up to changing 𝐠{\mathbf{g}}, we could have started with a parabolic subgroup BI𝐠\kern 0.5pt\vphantom{B}{}^{{\mathbf{g}}}\kern-0.5ptB_{I} where I=supp⁡(𝐛)=supp⁡(𝐛𝐠)I=\supp({\mathbf{b}})=\supp({\mathbf{b}}^{\mathbf{g}}). It also follows from Corollary 4.9(2) that 𝐛𝐠=𝐛𝝅I⁡(𝐠)​𝐰{\mathbf{b}}^{\mathbf{g}}={\mathbf{b}}^{\bpi_{I}({\mathbf{g}}){\mathbf{w}}} where 𝐰∈𝐖{\mathbf{w}}\in{\mathbf{W}} is an II-ribbon-II and where 𝐩=𝐠𝐰−1​𝝅I​(𝐠)−1{\mathbf{p}}={\mathbf{g}}{\mathbf{w}}^{-1}\bpi_{I}({\mathbf{g}})^{-1} is pure. In particular BI𝝅I⁡(𝐠)​𝐰=BIB_{I}^{\bpi_{I}({\mathbf{g}}){\mathbf{w}}}=B_{I} so 𝐠BI=𝐩BI\kern 0.5pt\vphantom{B}{}^{{\mathbf{g}}}\kern-0.5ptB_{I}=\kern 0.5pt\vphantom{B}^{{\mathbf{p}}}\kern-0.5ptB_{I}. We have 𝐛∈BI∩𝐩BI=𝝅I⁡(𝐩)(BI∩𝐭I​(𝐩)BI)=𝝅I⁡(𝐩)CBI(𝐭I(𝐩))=CBI(𝐩𝝅I(𝐩)−1){\mathbf{b}}\in B_{I}\cap\kern 0.5pt\vphantom{B}^{{\mathbf{p}}}\kern-0.5ptB_{I}=\kern 0.5pt\vphantom{(}^{\bpi_{I}({\mathbf{p}})}\kern-0.5pt(B_{I}\cap\kern 0.5pt\vphantom{B}^{{\mathbf{t}}_{I}({\mathbf{p}})}\kern-0.5ptB_{I})=\kern 0.5pt\vphantom{C}^{\bpi_{I}({\mathbf{p}})}\kern-0.5ptC_{B_{I}}({\mathbf{t}}_{I}({\mathbf{p}}))=C_{B_{I}}({\mathbf{p}}\bpi_{I}({\mathbf{p}})^{-1}), the second equality by Proposition 0.4, thus 𝐛{\mathbf{b}} commutes to 𝐩​𝝅I​(𝐩)−1{\mathbf{p}}\bpi_{I}({\mathbf{p}})^{-1}. Now 𝐩​𝝅I​(𝐩)−1BI=𝐩BI\kern 0.5pt\vphantom{B}{}^{{\mathbf{p}}\bpi_{I}({\mathbf{p}})^{-1}}\kern-0.5ptB_{I}=\kern 0.5pt\vphantom{B}^{{\mathbf{p}}}\kern-0.5ptB_{I}. Replacing 𝐩{\mathbf{p}} by 𝐩​𝝅I​(𝐩)−1{\mathbf{p}}\bpi_{I}({\mathbf{p}})^{-1} we get that any minimal parabolic subgroup containing 𝐛{\mathbf{b}} is as in the statement.

To show that these parabolic subgroups are actually minimal it is sufficient to show that Bsupp⁡(𝐛)B_{\supp({\mathbf{b}})} is a minimal parabolic subgroup containing 𝐛{\mathbf{b}}. By what we have just seen, any minimal parabolic subgroup of Bsupp⁡(𝐛)B_{\supp({\mathbf{b}})} containing 𝐛{\mathbf{b}} is of the form Bsupp⁡(𝐛)𝐩\kern 0.5pt\vphantom{B}{}^{{\mathbf{p}}}\kern-0.5ptB_{\supp({\mathbf{b}})} with 𝐩∈Psupp⁡(𝐛){\mathbf{p}}\in P_{\supp({\mathbf{b}})} and 𝝅supp⁡(𝐛)⁡(𝐩)=1\bpi_{\supp({\mathbf{b}})}({\mathbf{p}})=1, so 𝐩=1{\mathbf{p}}=1. ∎

Since minimality of parabolic subgroups transfers by conjugation, Proposition 4.12 proves the existence of a minimal parabolic subgroup containing any given element.

If the intersection of two parabolic subgroups is parabolic, there exists a unique minimal parabolic subgroup containing an element. Thus the validity of the following conjecture is supported by the results of [1, 6, 7, 8, 17]

Conjecture 4.13.

There exists a unique minimal parabolic subgroup containing a given 𝐛∈B{\mathbf{b}}\in B.

The following conjecture generalises Proposition 4.5, replacing HIH_{I} by 𝝅I\bpi_{I}. Note that for a positive element, HIH_{I} is a prefix of 𝝅I\bpi_{I}.

Conjecture 4.14.

Let 𝐛∈B{\mathbf{b}}\in B such that ℓ𝐒±1​(𝐛){\ell_{{\mathbf{S}}^{\pm 1}}}({\mathbf{b}}) is minimal in Conj⁡(𝐛)\conj({\mathbf{b}}). Then any 𝐩∈P{\mathbf{p}}\in P which centralises 𝐛{\mathbf{b}} and is such that 𝛑supp⁡(𝐛)⁡(𝐩)=1\bpi_{\supp({\mathbf{b}})}({\mathbf{p}})=1 centralises Bsupp⁡(𝐛)B_{\supp({\mathbf{b}})}.

Remark 4.15.

The ℓ𝐒±1{\ell_{{\mathbf{S}}^{\pm 1}}}-minimality assumption in Conjecture 4.14 is necessary. In the braid group of 𝔖4\mathfrak{S}_{4} with 𝐒={𝐬,𝐭,𝐮}{\mathbf{S}}=\{{\mathbf{s}},{\mathbf{t}},{\mathbf{u}}\} take 𝐛=𝐬𝐭{\mathbf{b}}={\mathbf{s}}^{\mathbf{t}}, I=supp⁡(𝐛)={𝐬,𝐭}I=\supp({\mathbf{b}})=\{{\mathbf{s}},{\mathbf{t}}\}, and 𝐩=(𝐮2)𝐭{\mathbf{p}}=({\mathbf{u}}^{2})^{\mathbf{t}}. Then 𝛑I⁡(𝐩)=𝛑Ir⁡(𝐩)=1\bpi_{I}({\mathbf{p}})=\bpi^{r}_{I}({\mathbf{p}})=1 and 𝐛𝐩=𝐛{\mathbf{b}}^{\mathbf{p}}={\mathbf{b}} but 𝐩{\mathbf{p}} does not centralise 𝐬{\mathbf{s}} or 𝐭{\mathbf{t}}.

Proposition 4.16.

Conjectures 4.13 and 4.14 are equivalent.

Proof.

Assuming Conjecture 4.13, if 𝐛{\mathbf{b}} and 𝐩{\mathbf{p}} are as in 4.14, then by Proposition 4.12 BIB_{I} and BI𝐩\kern 0.5pt\vphantom{B}{}^{{\mathbf{p}}}\kern-0.5ptB_{I}, where I=supp⁡(𝐛)I=\supp({\mathbf{b}}), are two minimal parabolic subgroups containing 𝐛{\mathbf{b}}, hence they are equal and by Proposition 0.4 𝐩{\mathbf{p}} centralises BIB_{I}, whence Conjecture 4.14.

We prove the converse. Up to conjugating 𝐛{\mathbf{b}}, we can assume that ℓ𝐒±1​(𝐛){\ell_{{\mathbf{S}}^{\pm 1}}}({\mathbf{b}}) is minimal in ConjB⁡(𝐛)\conj_{B}({\mathbf{b}}). Then, by Proposition 4.12, the minimal parabolic subgroups containing 𝐛{\mathbf{b}} are the Bsupp⁡(𝐛)𝐩\kern 0.5pt\vphantom{B}{}^{{\mathbf{p}}}\kern-0.5ptB_{\supp({\mathbf{b}})} for 𝐩{\mathbf{p}} in CP​(𝐛)C_{P}({\mathbf{b}}) such that 𝝅supp⁡(𝐛)⁡(𝐩)=1\bpi_{\supp({\mathbf{b}})}({\mathbf{p}})=1. By Conjecture 4.14, 𝐩{\mathbf{p}} centralises Bsupp⁡(𝐛)B_{\supp({\mathbf{b}})}. We deduce that Bsupp⁡(𝐛)=𝐩Bsupp⁡(𝐛)B_{\supp({\mathbf{b}})}=\kern 0.5pt\vphantom{B}^{{\mathbf{p}}}\kern-0.5ptB_{\supp({\mathbf{b}})} is the only minimal parabolic subgroup containing 𝐛{\mathbf{b}}. ∎

Given a Coxeter system (W,S)(W,S) and a pair (I,J)(I,J) with I,J⊆SI,J\subseteq S, we define the ribbon isomorphism problem in WW for (I,J)(I,J) to be the following problem: determine all the bijective maps φ:J→I\varphi:J\to I that extend to an isomorphism φw:WJ→WI\varphi_{w}:W_{J}\to W_{I} such that ww is a II-ribbon-JJ in WW.

Proposition 4.17.

Assume Λ\Lambda is a non-empty set of subsets of SS such that for any II in Λ\Lambda, the word problem and the conjugacy problem are solvable in BIB_{I} and the ribbon isomorphism problem is solvable in WW for any pair (I,J)(I,J) in Λ\Lambda. Then the two following problems are solvable.

  1. (1)

    Given II in Λ\Lambda and a word bb on 𝐈±1{\mathbf{I}}^{\pm 1}, decide whether the word bb represents the unity in BB.

  2. (2)

    Given two finite subsets I,JI,J in Λ\Lambda and words i,ji,j on 𝐈±1{\mathbf{I}}^{\pm 1} and 𝐉±1{\mathbf{J}}^{\pm 1}, respectively, decide whether or not ii and jj represent conjugate elements in BB.

Moreover, if the solution to the conjugacy problem in each parabolic subgroup BIB_{I} with I∈ΛI\in\Lambda provides a conjugating element, then the solution of problem (2) provides a conjugating element in BB too.

Proof.

Solution to problem (1) is clear as BIB_{I} embeds in BB and we have a solution to the word problem in BIB_{I}. Given ii and jj as in (2), denote by 𝐢{\mathbf{i}} and 𝐣{\mathbf{j}} the elements represented by ii and jj, respectively. By the solution to the conjugacy problem in the parabolic subgroup BIB_{I}, by testing for conjugacy the words in (𝐈±1)∗({\mathbf{I}}^{\pm 1})^{*} of length less than or equal to that of a word for 𝐢{\mathbf{i}}, we can find a representative word on 𝐈±1{\mathbf{I}}^{\pm 1} for each element 𝐢′∈BI{\mathbf{i}}^{\prime}\in B_{I} that is conjugate to 𝐢{\mathbf{i}} and such that ℓ𝐈±1​(𝐢′)\ell_{{\mathbf{I}}^{\pm 1}}({\mathbf{i}}^{\prime}) is minimal in ConjBI⁡(𝐢)\conj_{B_{I}}({\mathbf{i}}). By Proposition 4.7, ℓ𝐈±1​(𝐢′)=ℓ𝐒±1​(𝐢′)\ell_{{\mathbf{I}}^{\pm 1}}({\mathbf{i}}^{\prime})={\ell_{{\mathbf{S}}^{\pm 1}}}({\mathbf{i}}^{\prime}) and by Proposition 4.10, ℓ𝐒±1​(𝐢′){\ell_{{\mathbf{S}}^{\pm 1}}}({\mathbf{i}}^{\prime}) is also minimal in ConjB⁡(𝐢)\conj_{B}({\mathbf{i}}). Similarly, we can find a representative word on 𝐉±1{\mathbf{J}}^{\pm 1} for an element 𝐣′∈BJ{\mathbf{j}}^{\prime}\in B_{J} that is conjugate to 𝐣{\mathbf{j}} and such that ℓ𝐉±1​(𝐣′)\ell_{{\mathbf{J}}^{\pm 1}}({\mathbf{j}}^{\prime}) is minimal in ConjBJ⁡(𝐣)\conj_{B_{J}}({\mathbf{j}}). Again, ℓ𝐒±1​(𝐣′){\ell_{{\mathbf{S}}^{\pm 1}}}({\mathbf{j}}^{\prime}) is minimal in ConjB⁡(𝐣)\conj_{B}({\mathbf{j}}). Now 𝐢{\mathbf{i}} and 𝐣{\mathbf{j}} are conjugate if and only if some 𝐢′{\mathbf{i}}^{\prime} and 𝐣′{\mathbf{j}}^{\prime} are. By the proof of Proposition 4.10, some 𝐢′{\mathbf{i}}^{\prime} is conjugate to 𝐣′{\mathbf{j}}^{\prime} if and only if they are conjugate by the lift to 𝐖{\mathbf{W}} of some I′I^{\prime}-ribbon-J′J^{\prime} in WW where J′J^{\prime} is the support of 𝐣′{\mathbf{j}}^{\prime} and I′I^{\prime} is the support of 𝐢′{\mathbf{i}}^{\prime}. Since the ribbon isomorphism problem is solvable in WW for any pair (I,J)(I,J) in Λ\Lambda, we are done. ∎

When SS is finite the hypothesis concerning the ribbon isomorphism problem is always satisfied as stated in the following result. As a consequence, we get Proposition 0.7.

Proposition 4.18.

Assume (W,S)(W,S) is a Coxeter system with SS finite. The ribbon isomorphism problem is solvable in WW for any pair (I,J)(I,J) with I,J⊆SI,J\subseteq S.

Proof.

Let I,J⊆SI,J\subseteq S. Let Λ\Lambda denote the set of subsets I′⊆SI^{\prime}\subseteq S whose Coxeter graph is isomorphic to the Coxeter graph of II, and let ss be the number of graph automorphisms of the Coxeter graph of II. Since SS and II are finite it takes finite time to compute Λ\Lambda and ss. Any one-to-one map φ:I′→I\varphi:I^{\prime}\to I that extends to an isomorphism φ:WI′→WI\varphi:W_{I^{\prime}}\to W_{I} has to induce a isomorphism of graphs. So the set Λ~\tilde{\Lambda} of pairs (I′,φ)(I^{\prime},\varphi) such that φ:I′→I\varphi:I^{\prime}\to I extends to an isomorphism φ:WI′→WI\varphi:W_{I^{\prime}}\to W_{I} is finite and its cardinality is bounded by |Λ|×s|\Lambda|\times s. On the other hand, every ribbon can be decomposed into a finite product of elementary ribbons (I′,v⁡[s,I′′],I′′)(I^{\prime},v[s,I^{\prime\prime}],I^{\prime\prime}) (see [4, Proposition 2.3] and the set of elementary ribbons is finite (its cardinality is at most |S−I|×|Λ||S-I|\times|\Lambda|); the set of associated isomorphisms is easy to determine. Now, consider the finite oriented labelled graph with vertex set Λ~\tilde{\Lambda} and such that there is an edge from (I′,φ′)(I^{\prime},\varphi^{\prime}) to (I′′,φ′′)(I^{\prime\prime},\varphi^{\prime\prime}) labelled by the elementary I′I^{\prime}-ribbon-I′′I^{\prime\prime} τ\tau if φ′′=φ′∘φτ\varphi^{\prime\prime}=\varphi^{\prime}\circ\varphi_{\tau}. Then any II-ribbon can be read as a path in this graph based at (I,Id)(I,\Id), and any path without loop has a length of at most |Λ~||\tilde{\Lambda}|, which is less than |Λ|×s|\Lambda|\times s. So, computing all the isomorphisms that correspond to a path whose length is no more than |Λ|×s|\Lambda|\times s provides an answer to the ribbon isomorphism problem. ∎

5. A new topological version of the retraction

In this section we assume that SS is finite, since we use the results of [19]. We did not check whether Van der Lek’s results could be extended to infinite SS. According to Lemma 2.14, it is sufficient to define 𝝅I\bpi_{I} on the pure braid group and on simple braids to define it everywhere. We now give a topological definition of 𝝅I\bpi_{I} restricted to pr−1⁡(WI)\pr^{-1}(W_{I}).

Let VV be the reflection representation of WW, and VℂV_{\mathbb{C}} be the complexified space. The set TT is in bijection with the reflecting hyperplanes of WW. Let HsH_{s} be the hyperplane corresponding to s∈Ts\in T. We define X=V−⋃s∈THsX=V-\bigcup_{s\in T}H_{s} and similarly XI=V−⋃s∈TIHsX_{I}=V-\bigcup_{s\in T_{I}}H_{s}. Any element of VℂV_{\mathbb{C}} is of the form v=v1+−1​v2v=v_{1}+\sqrt{-1}v_{2} where v1,v2∈Vv_{1},v_{2}\in V. We write v1=ℜ⁡(v)v_{1}=\Re(v) and v2=ℑ⁡(v)v_{2}=\Im(v). Now, following Van der Lek, let 𝒞{\mathcal{C}} be the open Tits cone in VV and let Y={v∈X∣ℑ⁡(v)∈𝒞}Y=\{v\in X\mid\Im(v)\in{\mathcal{C}}\} ([19, II, (3.2)]). We define similarly YIY_{I} (note that though the Tits cone of WIW_{I} is bigger than 𝒞{\mathcal{C}} its intersection with XIX_{I} is the same). Choosing some y0∈Yy_{0}\in Y, the pure braid group is P=Π1​(Y,y0)P=\Pi_{1}(Y,y_{0}) and similarly the pure braid group of BIB_{I} is PI=Π1​(YI,y0)P_{I}=\Pi_{1}(Y_{I},y_{0}). There is a natural morphism P→PIP\to P_{I} (since Y⊆YIY\subseteq Y_{I}). We will show that this morphism is equal to 𝝅I\bpi_{I}. More generally, we have

Lemma 5.1.

Π1​(Y/WI,y¯0)≃pr−1⁡(WI)\Pi_{1}(Y/W_{I},\overline{y}_{0})\simeq\pr^{-1}(W_{I})

Proof.

We have the commutative diagram

1→P→B=Π1​(Y/W)→prW→1∥↑↑1→P→Π1​(Y/WI,y¯0)→WI→1\begin{CD}1@>{}>{}>P@>{}>{}>B=\Pi_{1}(Y/W)@>{\pr}>{}>W@>{}>{}>1\\ \Big\|@A{}A{}A@A{}A{}A\\ 1@>{}>{}>P@>{}>{}>\Pi_{1}(Y/W_{I},\overline{y}_{0})@>{}>{}>W_{I}@>{}>{}>1\\ \end{CD}

where each line corresponds to a covering. The vertical map in the middle is induced by the natural map Y/WI→Y/WY/W_{I}\to Y/W; it is injective since the left one is an isomorphism. This diagram proves the lemma. ∎

Proposition 5.2.

The natural morphism Π1​(Y/WI,y¯0)→Π1​(YI/WI,y¯0)\Pi_{1}(Y/W_{I},\overline{y}_{0})\to\Pi_{1}(Y_{I}/W_{I},\overline{y}_{0}) coincides with the restriction of 𝛑I\bpi_{I} to pr−1⁡(WI)\pr^{-1}(W_{I}).

Proof.

We prove that the two morphisms coincide on generators of pr−1⁡(WI)\pr^{-1}(W_{I}). By Lemma 2.19 this group is generated by BIB_{I} and the elements 𝐰𝐬2​𝐰−1{\mathbf{w}}{\mathbf{s}}^{2}{\mathbf{w}}^{-1} with 𝐬∈𝐒{\mathbf{s}}\in{\mathbf{S}} and 𝐰𝐬∈𝐖{\mathbf{w}}{\mathbf{s}}\in{\mathbf{W}} an II-reduced element. Let CC be the fundamental chamber in VV, that is the subset defined by αs​(x)>0\alpha_{s}(x)>0 for all s∈Ss\in S where αs\alpha_{s} is a linear form such that Hs={x∈Vℂ∣αs​(x)=0}H_{s}=\{x\in V_{\mathbb{C}}\mid\alpha_{s}(x)=0\}. The chambers are the images of CC under WW. Let FIF_{I} be the facet of CC defined by αs​(x)=0\alpha_{s}(x)=0 for s∈Is\in I and αs​(x)>0\alpha_{s}(x)>0 for s∉Is\not\in I. As in [19, II, Definition 4.8], we define Y⁡(I)Y(I) as the subset of YY formed of elements whose imaginary part is in FIF_{I} or in a chamber whose closure contains FIF_{I}. Then as a subgroup of Π1​(Y/WI,y¯0)\Pi_{1}(Y/W_{I},\overline{y}_{0}), the group BIB_{I} is the image of Π1​(Y⁡(I)/WI,y¯0)\Pi_{1}(Y(I)/W_{I},\overline{y}_{0}), and the natural morphism to Π1​(YI/WI,y¯0)\Pi_{1}(Y_{I}/W_{I},\overline{y}_{0}) is an isomorphism since Van der Lek [19, II, Proposition 4.9] shows that the inclusion induces a homotopy equivalence between Y⁡(I)Y(I) and YIY_{I}.

For the elements 𝐰𝐬2​𝐰−1{\mathbf{w}}{\mathbf{s}}^{2}{\mathbf{w}}^{-1}, we need to show that their image in Π1​(YI/WI,y¯0)\Pi_{1}(Y_{I}/W_{I},\overline{y}_{0}) is trivial. But we claim that the image is already trivial in the pure braid group Π1​(YI,y0)\Pi_{1}(Y_{I},y_{0}). This can be seen from the description in Van der Lek [19, I, Theorem 2.21 and II, Discussion 3.10] of such paths by galleries. The element 𝐬2{\mathbf{s}}^{2} corresponds to the gallery C,s​C,CC,sC,C. If s∉Is\not\in I the chambers CC and s​CsC are in the same chamber of YIY_{I} so that the gallery becomes trivial in YIY_{I}. By conjugation, the same happens to 𝐰𝐬2​𝐰−1{\mathbf{w}}{\mathbf{s}}^{2}{\mathbf{w}}^{-1}. ∎
